funded projects portfolio knowledge role pre-competitive knowledge production and diffusion system purpose translational r\&d, workforce development, industry-academia integration temporal dynamics multi-year lifecycle (planning → full operation → sustained funding) spatial embedding distributed across university campuses; industry geographically diverse governance model industrial advisory board (iab) with shared authority over research selection information flow bilateral and multilateral: academia ↔ industry ↔ nsf value exchange funding ↔ access to research ↔ ip rights ↔ talent pipeline basic structure - university-led center: a university (or consortium of universities) hosts the center. - industry members: companies and organizations become members by paying annual fees and participating in research planning. - nsf funding: the nsf provides seed funding and support to establish the center, with the goal of becoming self-sustaining. - collaborative research: projects are jointly proposed, selected, and executed by academic researchers and industry members. funding model source purpose ---------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------- 🧑‍🔬 nsf grant seed funding (e.g., planning grant, startup funding) 🏢 industry fees main ongoing support (membership dues) 🏛️ university support facilities, admin, partial staffing 🔁 matching or leveraged funds from state agencies, federal labs, other grants project lifecycle & governance center formation - universities apply for nsf planning grant. - recruit industrial partners. - host a planning meeting to align interests. operational model - research projects are proposed by university faculty. - industry advisory board (iab) (composed of member companies) votes on which projects to fund. - projects must be pre-competitive, meaning results are shared openly among members. execution - faculty and graduate students carry out the research. - industry mentors often provide guidance and real-world data. intellectual property (ip) - results are published or shared with all members. - members receive non-exclusive, royalty-free licenses. - additional rights (e.g., exclusive licenses) may be negotiated. references - industry-university cooperative research centers (iucrc) - centers

notes.text: social group : 12 in the social sciences, a social group can be defined as two or more people interacting, sharing similar characteristics, and collectively having a sense of unity. regardless, social groups come in a myriad of sizes and varieties. for example, a society can be viewed as a large social group. the system of behaviors and psychological processes occurring within or between social groups is known as group dynamics. in this note, we will explore the emergent phenomena of collections of humans interacting together. some of the interesting questions about social groups include: - ¿how does the size of the group impact its properties? - ¿how does collective intelligence making take place? - ¿how to design reputation systems? - ¿how influence works in groups? - in social networks; ¿which topics have become trendy? - ¿how do prediction markets aggregate knowledge? - how does consensus arise in groups? on effects of the group size - what is the ringelmann effect? - what is the name of the following effect: “tendency for individual members of a group to become increasingly less productive as the size of their group increases”? - the ringelmann effect references - wikipedia. notes.title: Human
notes.text: human a human is a member of the species homo sapiens, a highly evolved primate distinguished by advanced cognitive abilities, upright posture, complex language, and the capacity for abstract thought, culture, and technology. humans are social beings, capable of forming complex societies, creating institutions, and influencing their environment through tools and collective action. when born, one exists as a proto-human being—a repository of potentialities and developmental paths. one is not yet a “fully human” agent in terms of capacities, understanding, or self-realization. thought, action, and social interaction gradually shape which potentials are realized, guiding the emergence of distinct modes of human existence. over time, however, one can become locked into a particular mode of being, often reinforced by material constraints such as money. to explore different modes of human existence, one needs the courage to experiment and the ability to break free from limiting structures, pursuing a fuller range of human possibilities, so as to live one complete life rather than experiencing many small deaths along the way. qa: - what are the different modes of human being? what are the degrees of freedom of development? - is conceptualization necessary to distinguish specific modes of human existence, rather than merely acknowledging humanity in general? definition area definition ---------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ biology humans are complex multicellular organisms of the species homo sapiens , characterized by advanced brain development, upright posture, and complex organ systems that sustain life. cognition (psychology) humans possess advanced cognitive capacities, including reasoning, memory, learning, problem-solving, language, and self-awareness. behavior humans engage in purposeful actions guided by goals, emotions, habits, and social norms, influencing both individual and collective outcomes. society humans exist within structured social and cultural systems, creating institutions, norms, beliefs, and practices that shape interactions and collective life. health humans require physical, mental, and social well-being to function optimally, including nutrition, exercise, mental health, and social support. morality humans are capable of moral reasoning, evaluating actions as right or wrong, and creating ethical frameworks that guide behavior. social capital social capital is a form of energy that gives rise to a society. social capital refers to the value derived from individuals' social networks and connections. it encompasses the relationships, trust, and social norms between people and within communities. social capital is a resource that individuals and communities can draw upon to achieve their goals, whether they are personal, social, or economic. it can manifest in different forms, such as social support, information sharing, and collaboration, and can be built through social activities such as volunteering, community involvement, and networking. some benefits of social capital include access to information and resources, increased social support, improved health outcomes, and more significant economic opportunities. on the other hand, a lack of social capital can result in social isolation, limited options, and increased vulnerability. instead of socializing capital , it's about capitalizing on the social . therefore, it's necessary to coordinate education and work, foster a new entrepreneurial culture, and drive science and technology forward. human capital human capital refers to the aggregate stock of knowledge, skills, competencies, and attributes possessed by individuals or groups that enable them to perform productive activities, innovate, and contribute to social and economic processes. it is both an individual asset and a collective resource , developed through education, training, experience, and health, and crucial for the functioning and advancement of social systems. key aspects aspect explanation ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- intangible asset unlike physical capital, it consists of cognitive and embodied capacities. investment-driven accumulated through education, training, and socialization processes. productivity link enhances individuals’ and groups’ ability to generate economic value and social innovation. social embeddedness developed and realized within social institutions, cultural contexts, and networks. dynamic subject to growth, depreciation, and renewal over time. references - social capital - notes.title: Alan Curtis Kay
notes.text: alan curtis kay alan curtis kay is a prominent computer scientist known for his foundational contributions to the fields of object-oriented programming, graphical user interfaces (guis), and personal computing. here are some of his main works and contributions: 1. object-oriented programming : alan kay is credited with the conception of object-oriented programming (oop). this paradigm uses "objects" — data structures consisting of data fields and methods together with their interactions — to design applications and computer programs. kay's ideas about oop were realized in his development of the smalltalk programming language, which is one of the first and most influential object-oriented languages. 2. smalltalk : developed at xerox parc (palo alto research center) under kay’s leadership, smalltalk was pivotal in the evolution of modern computing, impacting the development of many contemporary programming languages and software methodologies. smalltalk was also one of the first programming languages to feature a completely integrated development environment (ide), influencing the user interface paradigms widely adopted later. 3. the dynabook concept : kay envisioned the dynabook in the 1970s, a personal computer for children of all ages. this concept was a precursor to the modern laptop and tablet and emphasized software that provided a dynamic medium for creative thought. the dynabook was intended to be a portable and accessible device that could handle dynamic simulations, multimedia content, and interactivity, significantly influencing the development of personal and educational computing. 4. graphical user interface (gui) : while at xerox parc, kay and his colleagues developed the concept of the graphical user interface, which uses windows, icons, menus, and pointers (wimp) to interact with computers. this development was revolutionary and formed the basis for interfaces in systems like the apple macintosh and microsoft windows. 5. contributions to education : kay has a strong interest in educational technology and how computers can be used as tools to enhance learning. he has been involved in various projects and research initiatives that explore how technology can transform education, reflecting his ongoing commitment to the dynabook's original vision. alan kay's work has been highly influential, earning him numerous accolades, including the turing award. his innovative ideas and developments have left a lasting mark on the way we interact with technology today. references - alan curtis kay -

notes.title: Alan Perlis
notes.text: alan perlis alan perlis was a pioneering computer scientist known for his influential work in the development of programming languages, particularly in the early days of computing. some of his main contributions include: 1. development of algol : alan perlis was one of the key figures in the development of the algol programming language, which was crucial in the evolution of high-level programming languages. algol greatly influenced many modern languages by introducing concepts such as structured programming and serving as a foundation for many subsequent languages like pascal, c, and java. 2. first recipient of the turing award : in 1966, perlis was awarded the first-ever turing award by the association for computing machinery (acm) for his influence on advanced programming techniques and compiler construction. 3. contributions to compiler construction : perlis made significant contributions to the field of compiler construction, which involves converting high-level programming languages into machine code that can be executed by a computer. 4. educational and professional leadership : as a professor and head of the computer science departments at carnegie mellon university and later at yale university, perlis was instrumental in shaping computer science education. his leadership helped establish the theoretical and practical foundations on which the discipline is based. 5. writings and aphorisms : perlis was known for his wit and wisdom, encapsulated in his well-known set of aphorisms about programming and technology known as "perlis's epigrams on programming." these epigrams are often quoted for their insight and humor regarding the nature of computing and programming. 6. research on artificial intelligence : he also contributed to early research in artificial intelligence, exploring how machines can simulate aspects of human intelligence. alan perlis’s work laid important groundwork for many aspects of computer science, particularly in the realms of programming language theory, compiler development, and the philosophical dimensions of computing. his legacy continues to influence both the practice and teaching of computer science today. references - alan perlis

"the strategy of economic development" (1958) : addresses economic development strategies and emphasizes the importance of unbalanced growth. 4. notes.title: Andrey Nikolaevich Kolmogorov
notes.text: andrey nikolaevich kolmogorov here's a table summarizing the major contributions of andrey nikolaevich kolmogorov , a prominent russian mathematician known for his foundational work in probability theory, topology, and turbulence: contribution description impact --- --- --- probability theory developed the modern axiomatic foundation for probability theory in his work "foundations of probability" (1933). established a rigorous mathematical framework for probability, making it applicable to various fields. kolmogorov complexity introduced the concept of algorithmic randomness and complexity, defining the complexity of a string based on the length of the shortest program that can generate it. laid the groundwork for information theory and the study of randomness in computer science. kolmogorov's continuity theorem proved the continuity theorem for stochastic processes, which ensures the existence of continuous paths for certain processes. fundamental in the study of continuous-time stochastic processes and brownian motion. kolmogorov-smirnov test developed the kolmogorov-smirnov test for comparing a sample distribution with a reference probability distribution. widely used in statistics for goodness-of-fit tests. kolmogorov equations formulated the kolmogorov forward and backward equations in the context of markov processes. essential for the study of markov processes and stochastic processes. turbulence theory made significant contributions to the theory of turbulence, including the statistical description of turbulent flows. advanced understanding of fluid dynamics and turbulent flow behavior. topology contributed to topology, including the study of topological groups and metric spaces. influenced the development of modern topology and its applications in analysis and algebra. functional analysis worked on functional spaces and operators, contributing to the theory of banach and hilbert spaces. impacted various areas of mathematics, including differential equations and quantum mechanics. ergodic theory developed ergodic theory, studying the long-term average behavior of dynamical systems. important for statistical mechanics and various applications in physics and engineering. kolmogorov's 0-1 law established a fundamental result in probability theory stating that certain events in a stochastic process have probabilities of either 0 or 1. key concept in the study of independent events and convergence in probability theory. random walks studied random walks and their properties, laying groundwork for later developments in stochastic processes. influential in various fields, including statistical physics and financial modeling. mathematical education and communication advocated for improved mathematical education and communication, writing extensively on mathematics pedagogy. contributed to the promotion of mathematics education in the soviet union and beyond. references - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/andrey kolmogorov

notes.title: Anthony Stafford Beer
notes.text: anthony stafford beer here is a table of stafford beer's main contributions, highlighting his key works, their publication years, and their contributions to the field of cybernetics and management science: year title contribution --- --- --- 1959 "cybernetics and management" introduced cybernetic principles to management, emphasizing the importance of feedback and control in organizations. 1966 "decision and control" explored the use of cybernetics in decision-making and control processes within organizations, laying the groundwork for managerial cybernetics. 1972 brain of the firm developed the viable system model (vsm), a theoretical model for understanding and designing effective organizational structures. 1975 "platform for change" discussed broader applications of cybernetics to societal and organizational change, advocating for systemic thinking and holistic management. 1979 "the heart of enterprise" expanded on the viable system model, providing detailed analysis and case studies of its application in various organizational contexts. 1981 "diagnosing the system for organizations" provided practical tools and methodologies for diagnosing and improving organizational effectiveness using the viable system model. 1985 "beyond dispute: the invention of team syntegrity" introduced the concept of team syntegrity, a structured approach for group decision-making and problem-solving based on cybernetic principles. 1989 "the viable system model: interpretations and applications of stafford beer's vsm" explored various interpretations and applications of the viable system model, demonstrating its versatility and effectiveness in different contexts. 1994 "beyond dispute: the invention of team syntegrity" (second edition) updated and expanded the original work on team syntegrity, providing further insights and applications. references - stafford beer - stafford beer open library! notes.title: Antonio Gramsci
notes.text: antonio gramsci here's a table summarizing the main ideas of antonio gramsci, an influential italian marxist philosopher and politician: main idea/concept description --- --- hegemony the concept that the ruling class maintains power not just through coercion but by achieving cultural and ideological dominance. cultural hegemony the process by which the values and beliefs of the dominant class become the "common sense" values of all, securing consent and stability. war of position vs. war of maneuver distinguishes between strategic, long-term cultural struggle (war of position) and direct, short-term revolutionary action (war of maneuver). organic intellectuals intellectuals that emerge from and articulate the interests of the working class, as opposed to traditional intellectuals aligned with the ruling class. historical bloc the alliance of different social classes and groups united by a common ideology or political project. passive revolution social change that occurs without a fundamental transformation of the dominant class's power structures. civil society and state differentiates between civil society (the realm of private organizations and institutions) and the state (political society), emphasizing the role of civil society in maintaining hegemony. prison notebooks a collection of essays written by gramsci during his imprisonment, covering his theories on culture, politics, and society. these ideas reflect gramsci's emphasis on the role of culture, ideology, and intellectuals in the struggle for social and political change. references - antonio gramsci

notes.title: Antonio Serra
notes.text: antonio serra the first economy development strategy. in the book ‘breve trattato,’ serra analyzes the economies of naples and venice to understand the prosperity of venice and the economic challenges faced by naples, which is rich in natural resources. his conclusions indicate that venice has a diversified economy characterized by activities that benefit from increasing returns to scale , whereas naples lacks this diversity; and decreasing returns . although antonio serra did not explicitly mention increasing returns , he implied this concept through his discussion of multiplicity in manufacturing . his analysis focused on the characteristics of manufacturing activities and how they contribute to economic dynamics . references - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/antonio serra - https://www.hetwebsite.net/het/profiles/serra.htm

notes.title: Bengt-Åke Lundvall
notes.text: bengt-åke lundvall bengt-åke lundvall, a prominent scholar in innovation and economic development, has contributed several key ideas to the field. some of his main ideas include: 1. national systems of innovation : lundvall emphasized the importance of examining innovation within the context of national systems, highlighting the interplay between institutions, organizations, and networks in fostering innovation and economic growth. 2. interactive learning : he introduced the concept of interactive learning, emphasizing that innovation is not just about r&d activities but also involves continuous learning processes that occur through interaction and collaboration among various actors, such as firms, universities, and government agencies. 3. innovation policy : lundvall's work has influenced discussions on innovation policy by advocating for policies that support knowledge diffusion, collaboration, and the creation of conducive environments for innovation rather than focusing solely on r&d investment or technology transfer. 4. innovation and competitiveness : he explored the relationship between innovation and competitiveness, arguing that a nation's ability to innovate and upgrade its technological capabilities is critical for maintaining or enhancing its competitiveness in the global economy. 5. knowledge economy : lundvall contributed to the understanding of the knowledge-based economy, highlighting the increasing importance of knowledge and innovation as drivers of economic growth and development in contemporary societies. these ideas have had a significant impact on the study of innovation systems, economic development, and innovation policy, influencing both academic research and policymaking efforts worldwide.

notes.title: Cayo Julio César Augusto
notes.text: cayo julio césar augusto césar augusto, el primer emperador romano, fundó y reformó varias instituciones que fortalecieron el imperio y consolidaron su poder. aquí tienes una lista de algunas de las instituciones más importantes que estableció o reformó: 1. praetorian guard (guardia pretoriana) : una unidad de élite que servía como guardaespaldas personal del emperador. 2. cohortes urbanae (cohortes urbanas) : un cuerpo de policía militar encargado del orden público en roma. 3. vigiles (bomberos y policías nocturnos) : un cuerpo encargado de la lucha contra incendios y la seguridad nocturna. 4. aerarium militare (tesoro militar) : un fondo destinado a pagar las pensiones de los veteranos del ejército. 5. res gestae divi augusti (las acciones del divino augusto) : un documento autobiográfico que registraba los logros de augusto y servía como propaganda imperial. 6. senado reformado : augusto reformó el senado, reduciendo su tamaño y asegurando que sus miembros fueran leales a él. 7. imperial cult (culto imperial) : promovió el culto al emperador como una figura divina, lo que ayudó a consolidar su autoridad. 8. legiones reorganizadas : reformó y reorganizó el ejército romano, asegurando su lealtad al emperador. 9. reformas administrativas provinciales : mejoró la administración de las provincias, reduciendo la corrupción y aumentando la eficiencia. 10. sistema monetario unificado : introdujo una moneda estándar para facilitar el comercio y la economía en todo el imperio. 11. biblioteca palatina : fundó una biblioteca en el palatino que se convirtió en un importante centro de aprendizaje. 12. juegos y entretenimiento público : patrocinó numerosos juegos y espectáculos públicos para ganar el favor del pueblo. estas instituciones y reformas ayudaron a consolidar el poder de augusto y a establecer una base sólida para el imperio romano que perduraría durante siglos. ¿te gustaría saber más detalles sobre alguna de estas instituciones? notes.title: Daniel Kahneman
notes.text: daniel kahneman untitled untitled untitled main ideas daniel kahneman is a nobel prize-winning psychologist known for his work in behavioral economics and cognitive psychology. his main ideas revolve around the understanding of human decision-making and judgment, often highlighting the biases and heuristics that influence our thinking. here are some of his key concepts: 1. dual process theory : kahneman proposed that human thinking operates through two distinct systems: - system 1 : fast, automatic, intuitive, and emotional. it operates effortlessly and is prone to biases. - system 2 : slow, deliberate, analytical, and rational. it requires effort and conscious thought. 2. prospect theory : this theory, developed by kahneman and amos tversky, describes how people make decisions under uncertainty. it suggests that individuals do not always make rational choices based on expected utility, but instead evaluate potential losses and gains relative to a reference point. it also introduces the concept of loss aversion, where losses loom larger than gains of the same magnitude. 3. biases and heuristics : kahneman has extensively studied cognitive biases, which are systematic patterns of deviation from rationality in judgment. some notable biases include: - availability heuristic : people judge the likelihood of events based on how easily they can recall examples from memory. - anchoring and adjustment : people rely heavily on the first piece of information (the "anchor") when making decisions, even if it's irrelevant. - confirmation bias : the tendency to search for, interpret, or remember information in a way that confirms one's preconceptions. - endowment effect : people tend to value objects they own more than identical objects they do not own. 4. happiness and well-being : kahneman's research also delves into the psychology of happiness and well-being. he distinguishes between the experiencing self (the one that lives in the moment) and the remembering self (the one that reflects on past experiences). he argues that these two selves can have different perspectives on what makes a person happy. 5. behavioral economics : kahneman's work has had a significant impact on the field of behavioral economics, which integrates psychological insights into economic theory. his research challenges the traditional economic assumption of rational decision-making and provides a more nuanced understanding of human behavior in economic contexts. overall, kahneman's main ideas emphasize the limitations of human rationality and the various cognitive biases that affect our decision-making processes. his work has profound implications for fields ranging from economics and public policy to psychology and everyday life. references - hume considered this his best philosophical work. political discourses 1752 essays later combined with earlier essays as essays and treatises on several subjects . influential in economics. four dissertations 1757 essays includes the natural history of religion and of the standard of taste . the history of england 1754–1762 history a six-volume work covering from julius caesar to the glorious revolution. very popular in hume’s time. dialogues concerning natural religion posthumous (1779) philosophy/theology a fictional dialogue discussing arguments for the existence of god; published after his death per his request. my own life posthumous (1777) autobiography brief autobiography written shortly before hume's death. research domains 🧠 epistemology & human understanding - core concern : how humans come to know anything—our perceptions, beliefs, and ideas. - key works : - a treatise of human nature (1739–40), book i - an enquiry concerning human understanding (1748) - key contributions : - distinguished between impressions (vivid perceptions) and ideas (faint copies). - critiqued the notion of causality —argued that cause-effect is inferred through habit, not reason. - formulated the problem of induction : no logical proof that the future will resemble the past. 🧭 moral philosophy - core concern : the foundations of morality and ethical behavior. - key works : - a treatise of human nature , book iii - an enquiry concerning the principles of morals (1751) - key contributions : - morality is based on sentiment , not reason. - argued for moral sense theory —our approval/disapproval arises from feelings, not logic. - introduced the is-ought problem : one cannot logically derive what ought to be from what is. ⚖️ political economy & politics - core concern : nature of government, commerce, liberty, and economics. - key works : - essays, moral and political (1741–42) - political discourses (1752) - key contributions : - advocated for free markets and limited government intervention. - critiqued mercantilism; emphasized the role of commerce in stabilizing civil society. - precursor to classical economics; influenced adam smith. 🏛️ religion & theology - core concern : nature of religious belief, miracles, and arguments for god's existence. - key works : - an enquiry concerning human understanding , section x (of miracles) - the natural history of religion (1757) - dialogues concerning natural religion (1779, posthumous) - key contributions : - argued against the rational basis of religious belief . - asserted that reports of miracles are unreliable and driven by human credulity. - in dialogues , questioned the design argument , suggesting the world’s imperfections weaken the analogy to a divine creator. 📚 history & literature - core concern : british history and philosophical aesthetics. - key works : - the history of england (1754–1762) - of the standard of taste (1757) - key contributions : - produced a popular historical narrative that shaped british identity for decades. - in aesthetics, explored subjectivity in taste , while defending the possibility of shared standards through cultivated judgment. 🖋️ style & legacy - writing style : clear, elegant, and often conversational—distinct from the dense treatise . - legacy : - central figure in empiricism and skepticism . - major influence on kant , who said hume “awoke [him] from [his] dogmatic slumber.” - foundational thinker for modern cognitive science , moral psychology , and philosophy of science . references - the economic thought of david hume https://web.archive.org/web/20170809152329id /http://www.humesociety.org/hs/issues/v15n1/mcgee/mcgee-v15n1.pdf - david hume https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/david hume

notes.title: Edgar Morin
notes.text: edgar morin edgar morin is a french philosopher and sociologist known for his interdisciplinary approach to understanding complex systems and human society. his work encompasses a wide range of topics, but some of his main ideas include: 1. complexity theory : morin is a pioneer in the field of complexity theory, which examines how systems composed of multiple interconnected elements exhibit emergent properties and behaviors that cannot be understood by analyzing their individual parts in isolation. 2. holism : morin advocates for a holistic approach to knowledge that recognizes the interconnectedness of different disciplines and aspects of human experience. he argues against reductionism and encourages a more integrated understanding of reality. 3. transdisciplinarity : morin promotes transdisciplinarity as a way of transcending the boundaries between academic disciplines and integrating diverse forms of knowledge to address complex problems. he emphasizes the need for dialogue and collaboration across disciplines. 4. methodology of complexity : morin has developed a methodology of complexity that emphasizes the importance of embracing uncertainty, ambiguity, and paradox in the study of complex systems. he encourages researchers to adopt a reflexive attitude and to engage in recursive processes of inquiry. 5. humanism : morin's work is deeply influenced by humanistic values, including a concern for social justice, environmental sustainability, and the promotion of human flourishing. he calls for a more compassionate and ethical approach to social and political issues. 6. critique of modernity : morin offers a critical perspective on modernity, highlighting its tendency towards fragmentation, alienation, and ecological destruction. he calls for a rethinking of modernity that takes into account its unintended consequences and promotes a more sustainable and humane future. 7. epistemological shift : morin proposes an epistemological shift from a linear, deterministic view of knowledge to a more open-ended, dialogical approach that embraces uncertainty, diversity, and complexity. he argues for a humility in the face of the limitations of human understanding. overall, morin's work challenges conventional ways of thinking and encourages us to embrace complexity, uncertainty, and interconnectedness in our understanding of the world and our efforts to address its challenges.

notes.title: Ernst Jünger
notes.text: ernst jünger ernst jünger (1895–1998) was a german writer, philosopher, and intellectual whose work spans literature, political reflection, and philosophical essays. he is often considered one of the most controversial and complex figures of 20th-century germany because his life and writing intersected with war, nationalism, and technology in ways that resisted simple categorization. h domain - war and technology - known for stormy depictions of combat and the transformative effects of modern warfare. - explored the interplay between human experience and technological change. - individual vs. mass society - advocated for a kind of heroic individualism and personal discipline. - critiqued the leveling effect of mass society, bureaucracy, and modernity. - modernity and totalitarianism - though not a straightforward supporter of nazism, he flirted with nationalist ideas and engaged critically with totalitarianism. - later works reflect a philosophical grappling with technology, power, and societal change. - existential and metaphysical inquiry - explored questions of mortality, heroism, nature, and the “inner experience” of life under extreme conditions. key works 1. in stahlgewittern (storm of steel, 1920) - memoir of his wwi experience; famous for its unromantic, vivid portrayal of combat. - controversial for its seeming admiration of military virtues. 2. der arbeiter (the worker, 1932) - philosophical essay on the role of work and technology in modern society. - seen as a meditation on the technocratic state and mass society. 3. auf den marmorklippen (on marble cliffs, 1939) - allegorical novel interpreted as a critique of totalitarianism. - evokes the rise of oppressive regimes in a symbolic, literary manner. 4. eumeswil (1977) - dystopian/critical novel exploring individual autonomy in a decayed society. - introduces the concept of the “anarch,” a reflective, sovereign individual amidst chaos. references - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ernst j%c3%bcnger - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hklf73dpumg

notes.title: Event-Driven Microservices
notes.text: event-driven microservices an architecture entry: a system decomposed into autonomous services that communicate through an event log rather than synchronous calls. formulation what is this architecture? a set of independently deployable services, each owning its data, coordinated through published domain events carried by a durable log. services react to events; no service calls another synchronously in the steady state. what does it trade off? coupling for latency and complexity: producers never block on consumers, but delivery becomes at-least-once, ordering becomes partial, and debugging requires tracing across the log. schema evolution of events is the load-bearing discipline. references - designing event-driven systems (ben stopford, o'reilly)

notes.title: Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process (FLP)
notes.text: impossibility of distributed consensus with one faulty process (flp) michael j. fischer, nancy a. lynch, and michael s. paterson, 1985. the paper that bounds what agreement can achieve: in a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic algorithm guarantees consensus with even one faulty process. formulation what does the paper prove? that every deterministic consensus protocol has at least one non-deciding execution when one process may fail by stopping. asynchrony makes it impossible to distinguish a crashed process from a slow one, so the protocol can be delayed forever. why does it matter? it draws the boundary every later protocol designs against: paxos, raft, and pbft all escape through the exits flp leaves open — randomization, partial synchrony, or failure detectors. references - impossibility of distributed consensus with one faulty process (pdf)

notes.title: Franco Malerba
notes.text: franco malerba franco malerba is a prominent italian economist known for his significant contributions to the field of industrial dynamics and innovation studies. his main ideas and research focus on the evolution of industries, the role of innovation and technology, and the dynamics of market structures. here are some of his key concepts: 1. sectoral systems of innovation : malerba developed the concept of "sectoral systems of innovation," which refers to the patterns of innovation specific to a sector, shaped by three main elements: knowledge and technologies, actors and networks, and institutions. this framework helps in understanding how innovations emerge and diffuse within specific sectors. 2. technological regimes and innovation : he explores the idea of technological regimes — sets of opportunities, appropriatenesses, and factors influencing companies’ innovative activities. malerba studies how these regimes affect the behavior of firms, industry structures, and the nature of innovation processes. 3. market dynamics and industry evolution : malerba has extensively researched the evolution of market structures within industries, focusing on how innovation influences market dynamics, including the entry and exit of firms, and how these changes affect competition and industry consolidation. 4. the role of policy in innovation : his work also emphasizes the importance of policy in shaping innovation, suggesting that effective innovation policy needs to be tailored to the specific characteristics of each sector, including its technological opportunities and market conditions. franco malerba’s research provides valuable insights into the complexities of industrial dynamics and the pivotal role of innovation in economic development, contributing to both academic theory and practical policy formulation. references - franco malerba - paper - 20451 - fundamentals of innovation and industrial change

notes.title: Gaspar Melchor de Jovellanos

headings.text: 🌾 Principales reformas y propuestas agrarias de Jovellanos
1. **Abolición de la vinculación de la tierra**

notes.text: gaspar melchor de jovellanos "informe sobre la ley agraria" (1795) gaspar melchor de jovellanos (1744–1811), una de las figuras clave de la ilustración española , abordó la cuestión agraria en su célebre obra "informe sobre la ley agraria" (1795) . en este informe, propuso reformas profundas para modernizar la agricultura española , que consideraba atrasada y bloqueada por estructuras jurídicas y sociales arcaicas. --- 🌾 principales reformas y propuestas agrarias de jovellanos 1. abolición de la vinculación de la tierra - denuncia el sistema de mayorazgos, manos muertas y vinculaciones eclesiásticas (propiedad de la iglesia y órdenes religiosas), que impedían la libre compraventa y transmisión de tierras. - propone liberar esas tierras para que puedan ser productivas y circulen en el mercado . 2. fomento de la propiedad privada libre - defiende que los campesinos deberían tener la posibilidad de poseer su propia tierra . - considera que la propiedad privada es un incentivo esencial para la mejora agrícola. 3. crítica al régimen señorial - critica los privilegios feudales que impedían el desarrollo económico rural. - considera que el poder señorial es incompatible con el progreso ilustrado. 4. inversión en infraestructuras rurales - propone mejoras en caminos, canales, riegos y cercados , fundamentales para aumentar la productividad agrícola. - subraya la necesidad de intervención pública en obras de infraestructura rural. 5. educación y formación agraria - insiste en la formación técnica de agricultores y en la difusión de conocimientos científicos aplicados al campo. - cree que la ignorancia es una de las causas principales del atraso agrario. 6. liberalización de precios y comercio - propone eliminar trabas al comercio de granos (como tasas o restricciones de transporte). - confía en que el mercado libre corregirá los desequilibrios y fomentará la productividad. --- 🧠 fundamento ideológico - influido por la fisiocracia francesa , especialmente por quesnay y turgot: la riqueza nacional se basa en la tierra y su explotación racional. - sin embargo, jovellanos no es un revolucionario : sus reformas buscan armonizar tradición y modernidad , y conservar el orden social siempre que permita el progreso. --- 📚 obra clave - "informe sobre la ley agraria" (1795) encargado por la real sociedad económica de amigos del país de madrid. es un texto fundacional de la crítica al sistema agrario del antiguo régimen en españa. --- ¿quieres que lo compare con los fisiocráticos franceses o con otros reformistas españoles de su tiempo, como campomanes o floridablanca? references • gaspar melchor de jovellanos

notes.title: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
notes.text: georg wilhelm friedrich hegel georg wilhelm friedrich hegel (1770-1831) was a german philosopher and one of the most influential figures in the history of western philosophy. hegel's philosophical system is often called "hegelianism" or "hegelian philosophy." his work spans various disciplines, including metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, political philosophy, and the philosophy of history. the hegelian system can be technically described as a framework of structurally constrained development , in which reality —conceived as the absolute —is not a fixed totality but a self-developing , self-relating process governed by the immanent logic of the concept (begriff) . this development is dialectical , meaning each stage (being, essence, concept) unfolds through internally generated negations that are not merely oppositional but sublated (aufgehoben) —preserved, negated, and elevated within a higher unity. the system is closed in form but open in motion , wherein each category emerges necessarily from the instability of its predecessor through determinate negation , resulting in a hierarchy of increasingly self-reflexive structures. the process culminates in absolute knowing where the system achieves self-transparency , having reconstructed itself through every mode of its own becoming—logical, natural, and spiritual—thus uniting ontology, epistemology, and logic into a single, internally complete, dynamically unfolding structure. see my completes notes on the hegel system → ‣. work year title (english) original title area summary --- --- --- --- --- 1801 the difference between fichte's and schelling's systems of philosophy differenz des fichteschen und schellingschen systems der philosophie philosophical criticism early critique establishing hegel's distinct philosophical direction. 1807 phenomenology of spirit phänomenologie des geistes epistemology, metaphysics traces the development of consciousness toward absolute knowledge. 1812–16 science of logic (3 vols) wissenschaft der logik logic, metaphysics systematic development of pure thought: being → essence → concept. 1817 encyclopedia of the philosophical sciences (1st ed.) enzyklopädie der philosophischen wissenschaften systematic philosophy overview of hegel’s system: logic, nature, and spirit. expanded in later editions. 1820 elements of the philosophy of right grundlinien der philosophie des rechts political philosophy explores freedom, ethics, family, civil society, and the state. 1821 lectures on the philosophy of history ¹ vorlesungen über die philosophie der geschichte history, spirit history as the rational progression of spirit toward freedom. 1823–30 lectures on aesthetics ¹ vorlesungen über die ästhetik aesthetics development of art from symbolic to romantic forms. 1825–31 lectures on the philosophy of religion ¹ vorlesungen über die philosophie der religion theology, philosophy god's self-revelation through religion and history. 1830 encyclopedia of the philosophical sciences (3rd ed.) same as above systematic philosophy final edition, often used as a reference to hegel’s mature thought. 1831 lectures on the history of philosophy ¹ vorlesungen über die geschichte der philosophie history of philosophy interprets western philosophy as spirit becoming self-aware. ¹ posthumously published by students and editors (especially eduard gans and karl ludwig michelet), based on lecture notes. impact hegel's work has profoundly impacted subsequent philosophical thought, influencing thinkers such as karl marx, søren kierkegaard, and the existentialists. however, his ideas are also highly debated, and interpretations vary widely. the complexity and abstract nature of his writing contribute to ongoing discussions about the true meaning and implications of hegel's philosophical system . 📖 philosophy - direct heirs: marx, kierkegaard, nietzsche (partly reactive), heidegger, sartre, adorno, žižek. - hegelianism deeply split: right hegelians (theological, conservative) vs. left hegelians (revolutionary). 🛠 political theory - marxism as an inversion: material dialectics grounded in class struggle. - modern critical theory, postcolonialism (e.g., fanon), and political theology draw heavily on hegel. 🔬 science and systems theory - inspired recursive, dynamic models (e.g., cybernetics, autopoiesis). - logic of becoming and totality echoes in complex systems and evolutionary theories. 🛐 theology - seen as a christian heretic or a metaphysical theologian. - deep impact on process theology , liberation theology , and post-kantian theodicy . references - lee, otis. "method and system in hegel." the philosophical review 48.4 (1939): 355-380. - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/alexandre koj%c3%a8ve

notes.title: Gilbert Simondon
notes.text: gilbert simondon gilbert simondon (1924-1989) was a french philosopher and theorist known for his work in the fields of philosophy of technology, philosophy of science, and philosophy of individuation. some of his main ideas include: 1. individuation: one of simondon's central concepts is individuation, which refers to the process through which an entity becomes an individual with distinct properties and characteristics. this concept applies to both natural and artificial entities. simondon was interested in understanding how things come into being and acquire their specific identities. 2. technological mediation: simondon explored the relationship between technology and culture. he argued that technology is not just a tool or an external force but plays a fundamental role in shaping human experience and society. he examined how technological artifacts mediate our relationship with the world and influence the way we perceive and interact with reality. 3. transduction: simondon introduced the concept of transduction, which refers to the process of transformation and exchange of information between different levels of reality. it is a key idea in his philosophy of individuation, describing the dynamic interplay between different elements in the individuation process. 4. collective individual: simondon challenged the traditional understanding of individuality as a static and isolated state. he proposed the concept of the "collective individual," suggesting that individuals are interconnected and share common features. this idea extends to both human and non-human entities. 5. concretization and abstraction: simondon explored the relationship between the concrete and the abstract. he argued that reality involves a continuous interplay between these two modes, and understanding this dynamic can provide insights into the nature of being and becoming. 6. information and communication: simondon was interested in the role of information in the construction of reality. he analyzed how information flows through different levels of reality, shaping the individuation process and influencing the development of both natural and technological entities. references - [ ] gilbert simondon - [ ] https://monoskop.org/images/2/20/simondon gilbert on the mode of existence of technical objects part i alt.pdf

notes.title: Giovanni Botero
notes.text: giovanni botero giovanni botero was an italian philosopher, priest, and diplomat known for his work in political theory and economics during the late 16th and early 17th centuries. his most famous work, "della ragion di stato" (the reason of state), laid the groundwork for many statecraft and political economy ideas. here is a table summarizing some of his key ideas: idea description --- --- reason of state botero introduced the concept of the "reason of state" concept, emphasizing that the state must act pragmatically to ensure its survival and prosperity, sometimes beyond moral or ethical considerations. population growth and state power he argued that a state's power and wealth are directly linked to population size and advocated for policies encouraging population growth. economic policy botero stressed the importance of economic strength for the stability and power of the state. he believed in fostering trade, industry, and agriculture. religion and statecraft while recognizing the importance of religion, botero argued that state interests should occasionally take precedence over religious considerations to maintain order and stability. moral philosophy despite advocating for pragmatism in state affairs, botero did not wholly abandon moral philosophy and believed rulers should still strive for justice and ethical governance where possible. balance of power he suggested that states should maintain a balance of power internally among various social classes and externally with other states to prevent any single entity from becoming too dominant. urbanization botero highlighted the significance of cities as centers of economic activity and cultural development, suggesting that their growth was vital for a state's prosperity. war and diplomacy he emphasized the strategic use of war and diplomacy, advocating for a combination of both to expand and protect state interests. national unity botero believed in the importance of national unity and the consolidation of power within a central authority to manage and grow the state effectively. role of the prince in his view, the prince or ruler should be wise, prudent, and strategic, embodying the ideals of both a just leader and a wise statesman. references - giovanni botero - …

notes.title: Heinz von Foerster
notes.text: heinz von foerster heinz von foerster's works are characterized by a deep commitment to exploring systems theory, cybernetics, and philosophy, with a focus on the interaction between humans, machines, and the environment. 1. cybernetics and self-organization von foerster was a major figure in cybernetics, the study of systems, communication, and control. his works often explore how systems, whether biological, mechanical, or societal, organize themselves without external control. he was interested in how systems maintain order and stability through internal feedback mechanisms and self-regulation. - self-organization : one of the central ideas in his work is the concept of self-organizing systems, where order emerges naturally through the interactions between components without requiring a central authority. this is a key feature in his later work, particularly in observing systems (1981). 2. the role of the observer a core element in von foerster’s philosophy is the idea that observation is always subjective and is an active, constructive process. he challenged the idea of objective, detached observation and instead suggested that the observer is an integral part of the system being observed. this idea is a cornerstone of his work in understanding understanding (2003) and his exploration of epistemology. - "the observer creates the observed" : von foerster famously argued that what we perceive as reality is shaped by the act of observation. this notion challenges traditional scientific views of objectivity and highlights the interplay between the observer and the observed in creating meaning. 3. communication and meaning von foerster believed that communication is fundamental to understanding how systems work. he explored how information is transferred and transformed, focusing on the relationship between communication and the observer. this theme is woven through many of his works, particularly in cybernetics of cybernetics (1974), where he delves into the recursive nature of communication and control. - constructivism : von foerster’s work has strong ties to constructivism, which holds that knowledge is actively constructed by individuals, not passively received. he was influenced by the idea that the act of knowing is an interaction between the knower and the known, rather than an objective capture of external reality. 4. ethics and philosophy von foerster’s work is also philosophical, particularly regarding the implications of cybernetic systems for human understanding and ethics. he was deeply concerned with the ethical responsibility of scientists and engineers in shaping systems, and he suggested that the creation of knowledge and technology should be done with awareness of its potential social and moral consequences. - the ethical responsibility of the observer : he argued that the observer bears responsibility not just for what they observe, but for how their observations shape the systems they interact with. this ethical dimension is present throughout his works, particularly in the broader context of the societal impact of technological systems. 5. complex systems and emergence von foerster’s later work also reflects an interest in complex systems, and how simple rules or components can give rise to complex, unpredictable behaviors. his exploration of how small, localized actions can lead to large-scale phenomena in systems is related to his work on self-organization and feedback. 6. interdisciplinary approach his works were deeply interdisciplinary, blending insights from philosophy, mathematics, biology, and engineering. this holistic approach allows for a deeper understanding of the interactions between different systems—be they biological, societal, or technological—and their implications for both theory and practice. references - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/heinz von foerster - von foerster, h. (1984). observing systems .

discusses aesthetics and teleology. 1790 religion within the bounds of bare reason ( die religion innerhalb der grenzen der bloßen vernunft ) explores the relationship between religion and morality, emphasizing rational faith. 1793 metaphysics of morals ( metaphysik der sitten ) comprehensive treatise on ethics and law, including duties, rights, and political philosophy. 1797 contribution contribution description --- --- metaphysics of the will schopenhauer posited that the underlying reality of the world is will , a blind, striving force manifesting in all phenomena, rather than rational or material structures. pessimism argued that life is fundamentally characterized by suffering because desire (will) is never fully satisfied; happiness is the temporary cessation of suffering. aesthetics and art proposed that art, especially music, allows temporary escape from the suffering of the will by offering contemplation detached from desire. ethics of compassion morality arises from recognizing others’ suffering and acting out of compassion rather than self-interest. influence on psychology anticipated ideas in psychology regarding the unconscious and the irrational forces underlying human behavior. influence on later philosophy strongly influenced nietzsche, freud, wagner, and later existentialist and pessimistic thought. references - https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/immanuel kant - https://archive.org/details/philosophyofkant01kant/mode/2up

notes.title: Jack Welch
notes.text: jack welch jack welch (1935–2020) was an american business executive best known for his role as chairman and ceo of general electric (ge) from 1981 to 2001. under his leadership, ge became one of the most valuable and admired corporations in the world. jack welch represents the high-efficiency, shareholder-focused capitalism of the late 20th century — admired for results, criticized for human cost. his tenure at ge is often seen as both a high watermark and a cautionary tale . 📈 career highlights - joined ge in 1960 as a chemical engineer. - became ceo in 1981 , succeeding reginald h. jones. - led ge until his retirement in 2001 . 🔧 management style and reforms 1. “fix, sell, or close” philosophy : - welch insisted that every ge business be #1 or #2 in its market , or it would be fixed, sold, or shut down. - this led to streamlining and downsizing , often aggressively. 2. rank and yank : - introduced a controversial performance management system: - top 20% of employees were rewarded. - middle 70% were encouraged to improve. - bottom 10% were let go. - criticized for creating a cutthroat culture . 3. delayering : - reduced layers of management to speed up decision-making and increase efficiency. - promoted a "boundaryless organization" , breaking down silos. 4. globalization & acquisitions : - pushed ge into financial services , media , and global markets . - expanded ge capital and acquired companies like rca (which owned nbc). 💰 results - ge's market capitalization rose from $12 billion to over $400 billion during his tenure. - became a management icon and was named “manager of the century” by fortune magazine in 1999. 📚 books - jack: straight from the gut (2001) – autobiography - winning (2005, with his wife suzy welch) – a business strategy book still widely read. 🧭 legacy and criticism positive : - revolutionized corporate efficiency. - inspired a generation of ceos with a clear performance-driven model. - built a leadership pipeline (many ge alumni became ceos elsewhere). negative : - criticized for short-termism and financial engineering. - ge’s overreliance on ge capital became problematic, contributing to the company’s later decline. - notes.title: James C. Scott
notes.text: james c. scott .. idea description --- --- high modernism scott critiques "high modernism," a belief in the ability to scientifically manage a society that often leads to authoritarian state projects that disregard local knowledge and customs. legibility and state control he argues that states attempt to make society "legible" by standardizing and simplifying complex social practices, which can lead to inefficiencies and resistance from local communities. anarchism and resistance scott explores how marginalized and oppressed groups resist state control and oppression through everyday resistance, such as foot-dragging, sabotage, and non-compliance. peasant studies in his work on peasant societies, scott emphasizes the importance of understanding peasants' economic and social practices, who often resist external control and exploitation. the moral economy scott introduces the concept of a "moral economy," where peasant communities prioritize social norms and subsistence ethics over market-based profit motives, challenging capitalist exploitation. critique of state-led development he critiques state-led development projects that ignore the local context and impose top-down solutions, often resulting in failures and harm to the people they intend to help. zomia and stateless societies scott studies the highland regions of southeast asia, known as zomia, where communities have historically evaded state control, maintaining stateless societies with their forms of governance. references - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/james c. scott

notes.title: Jan Hus
notes.text: jan hus jan hus was a czech theologian , philosopher, and reformer who played a significant role in the pre-reformation movement. his ideas and teachings laid the groundwork for future protestant reforms . here is a table summarizing some of his main ideas: idea description --- --- critique of the church hus criticized the moral and spiritual corruption within the catholic church, particularly the sale of indulgences and the luxurious lifestyles of the clergy. authority of scripture he emphasized the authority of the bible over church traditions and papal decrees, arguing that scripture should be the ultimate guide for christian faith and practice. preaching in vernacular hus advocated for preaching and conducting religious services in the vernacular language (czech), making religious teachings more accessible to the common people. reform of clergy he called for moral and ethical reforms within the clergy, demanding that they live piously and serve as true spiritual leaders. condemnation of indulgences hus vehemently opposed the selling of indulgences, viewing it as a corrupt practice that exploited believers and undermined genuine repentance. challenging papal authority he questioned the absolute authority of the pope, asserting that no human, including the pope, was infallible and that all must adhere to the teachings of the bible. salvation through faith hus emphasized that salvation is achieved through faith in jesus christ rather than through the intermediation of the church or the purchasing of indulgences. community of believers he promoted the idea of the church as a community of believers rather than a hierarchical institution, stressing the priesthood of all believers. ethical living hus encouraged ethical living and personal piety among christians, advocating for a return to the core values and teachings of christ. opposition to simony he condemned simony, the practice of buying and selling ecclesiastical positions, as a grave corruption within the church. jan hus's teachings and reforms were influential in the development of the hussite movement and had a lasting impact on the protestant reformation . his martyrdom for his beliefs also underscored the growing call for reform within the church . references - jan hus

notes.title: Jean-Baptiste Colbert
notes.text: jean-baptiste colbert origins: - maximilien de béthune, duke of sully , who served as the finance minister under henry iv, had earlier advocated for policies that promoted agricultural and industrial development. colbert built upon sully’s initiatives by further expanding industrial production and infrastructure. - colbert was aware of the dutch republic's and england's economic success, both of which had robust trading economies and advanced naval capabilities. he sought to emulate and surpass these by strengthening france’s navy and developing industries to compete in international markets. - state-sponsored innovation: colbert supported state-sponsored innovation and scientific advancement, similar to how other european nations were fostering scientific societies and technical advancements to boost economic growth. - colbert implemented policies that mirrored mercantilist principles by promoting exports , restricting imports through tariffs, and supporting the development of domestic industries to make france economically self-sufficient . here is a table summarizing key reforms implemented by jean-baptiste colbert during his tenure as the minister of finances under king louis xiv : reform implementation year key aspects impact and notes --- --- --- --- mercantilist policies 1661-1683 promoted state control over the economy, aimed at accumulating wealth through trade surplus strengthened the monarchy's financial position, increased state revenue through controlled industries manufacturing reforms 1660s-1680s established new industries, standardized quality, and increased production boosted france's manufacturing capacity, enhanced the quality of french goods for export infrastructure projects 1660s-1680s improved roads, canals, and ports to facilitate trade and commerce enhanced internal and external trade, reduced transportation costs trade protectionism 1664 imposed tariffs on foreign goods to protect domestic industries encouraged domestic production reduced competition from imports royal manufactures 1664 founded state-run factories to produce luxury goods like tapestries, glass, and silk centralized production of high-quality goods, boosted exports, and enhanced france’s global reputation tax reforms 1660s-1680s reorganized tax collection, reduced tax farming abuses increased state revenue, improved efficiency and fairness in tax collection navy expansion 1661-1683 built a powerful navy to protect french trade routes and colonial interests strengthened france’s naval power, secured trade routes, and supported colonial expansion colonial expansion 1660s-1680s promoted colonization in the americas, africa, and asia expanded french influence and control over valuable resources and trade routes commercial code 1673 codified commercial laws to regulate trade and business practices provided a clear legal framework for commerce, reduced disputes, and increased business confidence guild reforms 1660s-1680s regulated and controlled guilds to ensure quality and production standards standardized products, increased quality, and improved competitiveness of french goods attracting skilled immigrants 1660s-1680s encouraged skilled workers from other countries to settle in france enhanced technological expertise and boosted innovation within french industries jean-baptiste colbert, as the finance minister under king louis xiv, significantly influenced france's economic policies, including those related to research and development (r&d). although r&d in the modern sense wasn't as formalized in the 17th century as it is today, colbert's initiatives laid the groundwork for future scientific and industrial advancements. here is a table summarizing key aspects of jean-baptiste notes.title: Jerónimo de Uztáriz y Hermiaga
notes.text: jerónimo de uztáriz y hermiaga jerónimo de uztáriz, en su obra teórica y práctica de comercio y de marina (1724), propone fomentar industrias estratégicas que permitieran a españa recuperar su posición económica frente a potencias como inglaterra, francia y los países bajos. su selección se basa en criterios de utilidad nacional , valor añadido , empleo intensivo , potencial exportador y relevancia geopolítica . note: derive with chat gpt. 🏭 industrias seleccionadas para el fomento 1. textil (especialmente lana y seda) - considerada fundamental por su tradición en castilla y su potencial para generar empleo femenino y rural . - uztáriz propone mejorar la calidad , reducir la importación de tejidos extranjeros y fomentar la exportación a las colonias. - promueve el establecimiento de talleres manufactureros y el control de calidad artesanal . 2. construcción naval y marina mercante - industria clave tanto para el comercio exterior como para la proyección militar . - fomento mediante astilleros, subsidios, y formación de mano de obra especializada. - necesaria para sostener la relación comercial con américa y proteger las rutas marítimas. 3. metalurgia y armas - estratégica para la seguridad nacional y para abastecer la marina y el ejército. - uztáriz recomienda proteger la producción de hierro y acero , y evitar la importación de armas extranjeras. - también menciona el uso de minerales americanos para reducir la dependencia externa. 4. industria del papel y la imprenta - considerada clave para el progreso cultural , la administración pública y el control de la información . - fomento de molinos de papel y talleres tipográficos con materiales nacionales. 5. industria del vidrio y loza (cerámica) - sectores con alto valor añadido que competían directamente con productos importados de venecia y otras potencias europeas. - se recomienda proteger estas industrias por su valor artístico y comercial. 6. industrias derivadas de recursos coloniales - azúcar, tabaco, cacao, añil, entre otros, con procesamiento en la metrópoli para exportación con mayor valor. - fomento de fábricas locales para evitar que otros países refinen productos americanos . 7. agricultura transformada e industrias agroalimentarias - incluye producción de aceite, vino, harina y tejidos de lino o cáñamo . - uztáriz no ve la agricultura como opuesta a la industria, sino como una base necesaria para ella . ⚖️ criterios para su selección 1. reducción de importaciones y sustitución de productos extranjeros . 2. capacidad de exportación , especialmente hacia américa. 3. potencial de empleo intensivo . 4. interés militar o estratégico . 5. utilidad fiscal (industrias que generen ingresos tributarios). 6. existencia de materias primas nacionales o coloniales . references - notes.title: Joe Henrich
notes.text: joe henrich joseph henrich has proposed several models and theoretical frameworks throughout his academic work, largely focusing on evolutionary approaches to psychology, decision-making, and culture. his research encompasses a wide array of topics, including cultural learning, cultural evolution, culture-gene coevolution, human sociality, prestige, leadership, large-scale cooperation, religion, and the emergence of complex human institutions. some key concepts that henrich has explored in his published works include: 1. cultural evolution and group selection : he has discussed how cultural group selection plays a role in the evolution of cooperation and the development of complex societies. 2. cultural brain hypothesis : henrich has collaborated on work proposing the cultural brain hypothesis, which explores how culture drives brain expansion, sociality, and life history. 3. cumulative cultural evolution : he has explored how human beings accumulate cultural knowledge over generations and how this process can lead to complex cultural practices and technologies. 4. prestige and social learning : his work often references how individuals in societies use prestige as a cue for whom to learn from, thereby affecting cultural transmission and social hierarchies. 5. culture-gene coevolution : henrich has written about how cultural practices can influence genetic evolution, and vice versa, leading to a unique pathway of human development. 6. weird societies : he has written about western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic (weird) societies and how they differ psychologically from other societies around the world. henrich's models are often backed by empirical research, integrating ethnographic tools from anthropology with experimental techniques from psychology and economics. his areas of interest span several geographical locations, including amazonia, chile, and fiji, where he has conducted fieldwork to support his theories. for a comprehensive view of his contributions, one could delve into his wide array of publications which cover these models and theories in more depth【40†source】【41†source】【42†source】. references - joe notes.title: Johan de Witt
notes.text: johan de witt johan de witt was a prominent dutch statesman during the dutch golden age, serving as grand pensionary of holland from 1653 to 1672. he played a crucial role in the political and economic development of the dutch republic. here is a table summarizing some of his main ideas and contributions: idea/contribution description --- --- republicanism de witt strongly advocated for republican governance, opposing the house of orange's monarchical aspirations. he believed in the rule of law and governance by elected officials rather than hereditary rulers. economic policy de witt promoted free trade and supported the dutch maritime industry, which helped make the dutch republic a leading economic power. he emphasized the importance of a strong navy to protect trade routes. balance of power he worked to balance european power, forming alliances to counter the dominance of major powers like france and england. this included negotiating peace treaties and forming defensive coalitions. navigation act de witt opposed england's navigation acts, which restricted dutch trade. he sought to ensure open and free trade routes for the dutch fleet, emphasizing economic independence and strength. military strategy he believed in a powerful navy and a well-maintained army to defend the republic and its interests. he focused on modernizing the military and enhancing its strategic capabilities. political stability de witt aimed to maintain political stability within the dutch republic by managing internal conflicts and promoting unity among the provinces. he sought to balance the interests of various political factions. education and science he supported advancements in education and science, recognizing their importance for the progress and innovation of the dutch republic. fiscal responsibility de witt advocated for fiscal responsibility and efficient government spending. he implemented policies to manage public debt and ensure financial stability. tolerance and religious freedom although not universally tolerant, de witt promoted a degree of religious tolerance to maintain social peace and economic prosperity. he understood the importance of a stable and diverse society for economic growth. diplomacy de witt was skilled in diplomacy, often negotiating complex treaties and alliances to protect dutch interests and maintain peace. his diplomatic efforts were vital in navigating the turbulent political landscape of 17th-century europe. johan de witt's ideas and policies significantly shaped the dutch republic's political and economic landscape during his tenure, contributing to its status as a major european power in the 17th century. references - johan de witt

notes.title: Johann Friedrich von Pfeiffer
notes.text: johann friedrich von pfeiffer johann friedrich von pfeiffer , an influential german economist and public official in the 18th century, is known for his contributions to economic theory and policy, particularly regarding the relationship between agriculture and trade. here’s a table summarizing the main ideas of johann friedrich von pfeiffer : main idea description --- --- agricultural importance emphasized the central role of agriculture in a nation's economy, advocating for policies that enhance agricultural productivity as a basis for economic growth. mercantilism supported mercantilist principles, arguing that national wealth is best enhanced through a favorable balance of trade by maximizing exports and minimizing imports. economic policy recommendations suggested protective tariffs and subsidies to nurture domestic industries and agriculture, fostering self-sufficiency and enhancing the nation's economic position. critique of free trade acknowledged benefits of free trade but critiqued its potential adverse effects on local economies, including undermining domestic production and fostering dependency. social welfare highlighted the social implications of economic policies, arguing that a prosperous agricultural sector leads to improved living conditions and social stability. references - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/johann friedrich von pfeiffer - …

notes.title: Johann Heinrich von Thünen
notes.text: johann heinrich von thünen johann heinrich von thünen was a 19th-century german economist and agriculturalist known for his pioneering work on agricultural economics and spatial economics. here are the main ideas associated with his work: 1. the isolated state model thünen's most famous contribution is his model of the "isolated state," presented in his book "der isolierte staat" (the isolated state). this model analyzes the optimal use of land surrounding a central city, considering transportation costs and the perishability of agricultural products. it was one of the first spatial economic models and laid the foundation for location theory . 2. location theory thünen's model introduced the concept of location theory in economics. he proposed that different types of farming would be located at various distances from a central market based on transportation costs and the value of the land. for example: - dairying and intensive farming are located closest to the city because of high transportation costs and perishability. - forestry follows next because timber is bulky and costly to transport. - crop farming and grain production are farther away since these products are less perishable and cheaper to transport. - ranching and livestock raising are located farthest from the city due to lower animal transportation costs. 3. economic rent thünen introduced the concept of economic rent in his model. economic rent refers to the surplus income a farmer earns due to the advantageous location of their land relative to the market. the closer the land is to the market, the higher its economic rent due to reduced transportation costs. 4. marginal productivity theory thünen also contributed to the development of marginal productivity theory. he was among the first to describe the relationship between labor input and agricultural output. he suggested that labor productivity diminishes as more labor is added, a principle later formalized in neoclassical economics. 5. intensive vs. extensive agriculture thünen differentiated between intensive and extensive agriculture based on their proximity to the market and land use intensity. intensive agriculture, requiring more labor and capital per unit of land, is practiced closer to the market. in contrast, extensive agriculture, which uses larger land areas with less labor and capital, is practiced further away. 6. the thünen rings in his model, thünen visualized the land use around the central market city as a series of concentric rings, each dedicated to a specific type of agriculture. this spatial arrangement is driven by transportation costs and the perishability of goods, providing a theoretical explanation for land use patterns. sources: - wikipedia - johann heinrich von thünen - encyclopedia britannica - johann heinrich von thünen - econlib - johann heinrich von thünen thünen's work remains influential in economic geography, urban economics, and the study of land use patterns.
