notes.title: Mark Sanford Granovetter
notes.text: mark sanford granovetter mark granovetter is a prominent american sociologist known for his work in social networks and economic sociology. his research has significantly impacted our understanding of how social networks influence economic behavior, organizational structures, and the spread of information and ideas. here are some key ideas associated with mark granovetter: 1. strength of weak ties: granovetter introduced the concept of "the strength of weak ties" in his seminal paper titled "the strength of weak ties" (1973). he argued that weak ties—connections between individuals who are not closely connected or do not interact frequently—play a crucial role in accessing new information, resources, and opportunities. while strong ties (close friends, family members) provide emotional support and reinforce existing beliefs, weak ties facilitate the flow of novel information and ideas from distant parts of a social network. 2. embeddedness: granovetter's work emphasizes the idea of "embeddedness," which refers to how social relationships are intertwined with economic and organizational structures. he argued that economic action is embedded within social networks and institutions and that these social ties shape individuals' behavior, decision-making processes, and economic outcomes. granovetter's concept of embeddedness has challenged traditional economic models that assume rational, self-interested actors operating in isolation. 3. structural holes: building on the notion of social networks, granovetter introduced the concept of "structural holes" in his book "getting a job: a study of contacts and careers" (1995). he argued that individuals who bridge structural holes—gaps or discontinuities in a network between otherwise disconnected groups—have access to unique information, resources, and opportunities. these individuals can gain competitive advantages in job placement, innovation, and entrepreneurship by occupying brokerage positions between different social clusters. 4. network analysis: granovetter's work has contributed to developing network analysis as a methodological approach for studying social relationships and structures. network analysis involves examining the patterns of connections between actors in a social network, including the identification of key actors, subgroups, and network properties such as centrality, density, and cohesion. granovetter's research has demonstrated the importance of network structures in shaping individual behavior and collective outcomes. overall, mark granovetter's ideas have profoundly impacted multiple disciplines, including sociology, economics, management, and communication studies. his research has provided valuable insights into the role of social networks in economic life, the diffusion of innovations, the formation of social capital, and the functioning of organizations and markets. granovetter's work inspires scholars and practitioners to understand the complex interplay between social relationships, economic behavior, and institutional contexts.

notes.text: michał kalecki main ideas main idea description --- --- effective demand kalecki emphasized the role of effective demand in determining output and employment levels, similar to keynes. income distribution he highlighted the impact of income distribution between capitalists and workers on consumption, investment, and economic dynamics. business cycle theory kalecki developed a theory of business cycles based on the interaction between investment, profits, and changes in income distribution. degree of monopoly kalecki introduced the concept of the degree of monopoly, describing how firms with market power influence prices and distribution. fiscal policy he argued that government fiscal policy, including public investment and consumption, plays a crucial role in stabilizing the economy. investment decision-making kalecki analyzed the determinants of investment, emphasizing the role of profits and expectations in investment decisions. political business cycle he proposed that political factors, such as elections and government policies, can influence economic cycles and business conditions. class conflict kalecki integrated class conflict into his analysis, recognizing the differing interests of capitalists and workers in economic outcomes. critique of say's law he challenged say's law by arguing that supply does not automatically create its own demand, highlighting the importance of aggregate demand. imperfect competition kalecki's work incorporated the reality of imperfect competition in markets, contrasting with the traditional assumption of perfect competition. 🏗️ i. macroeconomic dynamics & business cycle theory 🔁 business cycle model - core idea: investment drives the cycle , not autonomous shocks. - key components: - investment is volatile due to expectations. - profits = investment + capitalists' consumption . - lagged adjustments in output and profits lead to cyclical fluctuations . - incorporates multiplier-accelerator dynamics . - technical structure: nonlinear difference equations with delayed investment response. 📉 crisis theory - crises are not anomalies—they are structurally embedded . - causes include: - declining investment. - falling profit expectations. - insufficient effective demand. - recurrent crises are tied to capitalist control over investment and underconsumption tendencies. 📊 ii. distribution & income theory 💸 profit equation one of his most famous insights: profits = investment + capitalists’ consumption + government deficit + net exports − workers’ saving - workers tend to spend all their wages (mpc ≈ 1). - capitalists save, so only their spending drives profits . - emphasizes a circular flow of income in a class-divided economy. 📐 markup pricing and income distribution - in oligopolistic industries, firms set prices via markup over costs: p=(1+μ)⋅unit labor costp = (1 + \mu) \cdot \text{unit labor cost} - distribution between wages and profits depends on: - the markup (μ) . - the degree of monopoly . - class bargaining power . - this forms the basis for his theory of income distribution . 🧰 iii. growth theory 📈 theory of economic dynamics (1954) - integrates short-term cycles and long-term growth. - growth rate depends on: - investment propensity (out of profits). - government policy (exogenous demand stimulation). - structural features like income distribution. - distinct from harrod-domar by being class-based and dynamic differently (not just knife-edge instability). 🏛️ iv. political economy 🧠 political aspects of full employment (1943) - anticipates modern political economy of macro policy: - even if full employment is possible , capitalists may resist it. - reasons: - loss of social control over workers. - weakened discipline in the workplace. - threat to ideological dominance . - insightful for understanding why capital resists keynesianism in practice. 🛠️ v. public finance and policy 💵 functional finance perspective - fiscal deficits are necessary and good under unemployment. - deficits should stimulate demand and reduce idle capacity. - anticipates lerner’s functional finance , but from a class-conflict perspective. 🛑 limits of monetary policy - kalecki was skeptical of monetary policy as a stabilizer. - interest rates affect investment weakly and unpredictably . - emphasis on fiscal policy and public investment instead. 🌍 vi. open economy and imperialism 🌐 external sector: net exports - net exports boost profits: profits=i+cc+g+(x−m)−sw\text{profits} = i + c c + g + (x - m) - s w - trade surpluses benefit capitalist profits, much like investment and deficit spending. 🛢️ colonialism and unequal exchange - early writings touched on how imperialism supports capitalist accumulation in core countries. - profits can be sustained by extracting surplus from the periphery. 📘 vii. key concepts and theoretical innovations concept description --- --- effective demand output is demand-constrained, not supply-constrained. investment-led profits "capitalists earn what they spend." class-based macroeconomics divides agents into classes (workers/capitalists) instead of representative agents. markup pricing prices set by firms over costs, not by marginal productivity. political constraints macroeconomic policy is limited by class conflict, not technical feasibility. references - michał kalecki - https://archive.org/details/selectedessayson0000kale/mode/2up

notes.title: Michael Hudson (Economist)
notes.text: michael hudson (economist) michael hudson, an economist, is known for several key ideas: 1. debt and financialization : hudson emphasizes the role of debt in modern economies, arguing that excessive debt burdens can lead to financial instability and economic crises. he criticizes financialization, where financial activities dominate the economy, often at the expense of productive sectors. 2. rentier capitalism : hudson discusses the concept of rentier capitalism, where wealth is derived primarily from ownership and control of assets rather than productive activities. he analyzes how rent extraction from land, natural resources, and intellectual property can exacerbate inequality and stifle economic growth. 3. historical analysis : hudson's work incorporates historical analysis to understand economic phenomena. he examines the role of debt, land tenure systems, and financial institutions throughout history, drawing parallels with contemporary economic issues. 4. critique of neoliberalism : hudson is critical of neoliberal economic policies, which prioritize deregulation, privatization, and austerity measures. he argues that such policies often benefit the wealthy elite at the expense of the broader population, leading to inequality and social unrest. 5. alternative economic policies : hudson advocates for alternative economic policies aimed at reducing inequality, stabilizing financial systems, and promoting sustainable development. these may include debt relief for struggling borrowers, public investment in infrastructure, and reforms to taxation and financial regulation. overall, michael hudson's work offers a heterodox perspective on economics, challenging mainstream theories and policies while emphasizing the importance of historical context and addressing systemic issues such as debt, financialization, and inequality. references - michael hudson (economist))

notes.title: Michael Porter
notes.text: michael porter michael porter is an influential economist, researcher, and professor at harvard business school known for his work in competitive strategy, business economics, and economic development. here are some of michael porter's main ideas: concept description --- --- porter's five forces framework analyzes industry competitiveness by identifying five forces: rivalry among competitors, threat of new entrants, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, and threat of substitutes. this framework helps businesses understand their competitive environment and develop effective strategies based on these forces. value chain analysis a method for examining a firm's activities to identify sources of competitive advantage, dividing them into primary activities (e.g., production, marketing) and support activities (e.g., hr management, technology). this analysis helps companies find areas for differentiation or cost leadership to enhance customer value. competitive advantage focuses on achieving a sustainable competitive edge, either through cost leadership (lower costs) or differentiation (unique offerings valued by customers). companies that successfully use these strategies can achieve higher profits and market share in the long term. clusters and economic development examines the impact of industry clusters—geographic concentrations of related companies and institutions—on productivity and competitiveness. clusters encourage knowledge sharing, collaboration, and innovation, leading to higher regional economic growth. porter advocates policies that support cluster development to drive economic prosperity. shared value emphasizes the importance of creating both economic value and social value by addressing societal needs and challenges through business practices. this approach aligns business goals with social and environmental objectives, supporting long-term sustainability and positive social impact. references - porter, m. e. notes.title: Milton Friedman
notes.text: milton friedman …. qa: - why milton win the “nobel memorial prize in economic sciences”? his achievements in the fields of consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and for his demonstration of the complexity of stabilization policy. - … monetarism - developed the monetary theory of inflation – "inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon." - argued for control of money supply growth to manage inflation. permanent income hypothesis - proposed that consumers base spending on expected long-term income rather than current income. - this fundamentally challenged keynesian models, which emphasized current income. - it reshaped how economists understand savings, consumption, and fiscal policy. critique of keynesian economics - challenged short-run stabilization policies. - emphasized market self-correction and limits of fiscal policy. natural rate of unemployment - introduced the idea that there's a minimum level of unemployment that cannot be reduced by monetary policy without causing inflation. policy advocacy - advocate of free markets , limited government , school vouchers , voluntary military , and deregulation . monetary history and theory - a monetary history of the united states, 1867–1960 (with anna schwartz): - this book argued that monetary policy (money supply management) had a central role in economic cycles. - their analysis of the great depression famously argued that it was worsened by poor monetary policy by the federal reserve. - this revived interest in the quantity theory of money and laid the foundation for monetarism . critique of stabilization policy - friedman showed that government efforts to stabilize the economy (e.g., using fiscal or monetary tools to smooth business cycles) often have unintended effects due to: - policy lags - inaccurate forecasting - market expectations - he argued that such policies could be destabilizing , not helpful. technical work 📘 technical books & monographs title year main contribution --- --- --- income from independent professional practice 1945 empirical study of income distribution and taxation among professionals a theory of the consumption function 1957 introduced the permanent income hypothesis studies in the quantity theory of money 1956 modern restatement and empirical analysis of the quantity theory of money a program for monetary stability 1960 advocated for rules-based monetary policy and monetary growth targeting a monetary history of the united states, 1867–1960 1963 showed that monetary forces drove major economic fluctuations, including the great depression the optimum quantity of money and other essays 1969 theoretical essays on money, including the friedman rule on optimal inflation monetary trends in the u.s. and the u.k. 1982 long-term analysis of money growth, inflation, and output in comparative context 📄 key technical journal articles title year journal main contribution --- --- --- --- the methodology of positive economics 1953 in essays in positive economics argued that predictive power , not assumptions’ realism, defines scientific value the quantity theory of money — a restatement 1956 in studies... empirical restatement of classical monetary theory money and business cycles 1953 review of economics and statistics linked money supply changes with business cycle fluctuations the role of monetary policy 1968 american economic review introduced natural rate of unemployment , critiqued phillips curve a monetary theory of nominal income 1971 journal of political economy modeled monetary effects on nominal gdp , challenged fiscal-dominant views references - notes.title: Nicolás de Cusa
notes.text: nicolás de cusa nicholas of cusa (also known as nicolaus cusanus) was a german philosopher, theologian, jurist, and astronomer, notable for his progressive thinking in the early renaissance period. one of his main works, which encapsulates his thinking and philosophical approaches, is "de docta ignorantia" (on learned ignorance). written in 1440, this treatise explores the limits of human knowledge and introduces the concept of "learned ignorance," which argues that true knowledge lies in recognizing one's own ignorance. key points about "de docta ignorantia": 1. coincidence of opposites : nicholas of cusa discusses the idea that in god, maximum and minimum coincide; thus, contradictions resolve in the divine essence. this notion is foundational in understanding his philosophical and theological exploration of the infinite. 2. god and infinity : he suggests that god, being infinite, cannot be comprehended fully by finite human reason. according to cusanus, all human concepts are mere approximations of the truth. 3. the pursuit of knowledge : the treatise argues that since true knowledge is that god is incomprehensible, the more one knows, the more keenly they become aware of their own ignorance. other important works by nicholas of cusa include: - "de concordantia catholica" (on catholic concordance): this treatise, written around the time he was involved in the council of basel, discusses the governance of the church and promotes the idea of conciliarism, advocating for a harmonious relationship between the authority of the council and that of the pope. - "de visione dei" (on the vision of god): known as the treatise on the "vision of god," this work is a spiritual dialogue that discusses god's omnipresence and how he can be seen in all things through a form of mystical seeing. - "de beryllo" (on [the] beryl): here nicholas of cusa uses the metaphor of a lens (beryl) to explain the process of intellectual insight into the nature of objects. nicholas of cusa's philosophical and theological thoughts were deeply influential, especially his ideas concerning the knowledge of god and the limits of human understanding. his works continue to be studied for their innovative approaches to philosophy, theology, and science. references - nicolás de cusa - …

notes.title: Nicolás Gómez Dávila
notes.text: nicolás gómez dávila nicolás gómez dávila , a colombian writer and thinker, is best known for his unique aphoristic style, blending classical conservatism with sharp, critical insights into modernity. his main works include: 1. "escolios a un texto implícito" (glosses to an implicit text) : this is his principal work, composed entirely of aphorisms and reflective notes. the text itself is 'implicit' as it never directly appears; instead, dávila's escolios (marginal notes or glosses) offer commentary on a wide range of topics, including philosophy, culture, politics, and religion. the work was published in several volumes from the 1970s to the early 1990s. 2. "textos i" : a collection of various writings that further explore themes similar to those in "escolios a un texto implícito." this compilation includes essays and aphorisms that delve into dávila's critique of modern society and his conservative, sometimes reactionary, viewpoints. dávila's work is characterized by its brevity, depth, and a tendency to challenge conventional wisdom. his writings are highly regarded in certain intellectual circles for their incisive analysis and the elegance of their expression, although they have not always been widely accessible due to the unique nature of his work and his preference for privacy and seclusion from public life. references - nicolás gómez dávila

headings.text: Can Chomsky be categorized as someone from the symbolic view of Cognitive Science?

notes.text: noam chomsky a language is, according to chomsky, a state obtained by a specific mental computational system that develops naturally and whose exact parameters are set by the linguistic environment that the individual is exposed to as a child. this definition, which is at odds with the common notion of a language as a public system of verbal signals shared by a group of speakers, has important implications for the nature of the mind. note: the constant thread in chomsky’s work is a single question: what is the nature of the language faculty as a neural-biological system, and how can it be explained? his proposal has changed, etc. language language is a species-specific, biologically endowed computational system (i-language) that generates structured pairings of sound and meaning via universal grammar, emerging in the mind/brain and acquired through parameter-setting from limited input. grammar for chomsky, a grammar is not “grammar” in the everyday sense of prescriptive rules, but a formal, explicit theory of a language . technically, in his framework: - grammar = the internalized cognitive system (i-language) in a speaker’s mind/brain that generates all and only the well-formed sentences of that language. - it is a generative system : a finite set of rules or principles that can produce (generate) an infinite set of possible sentences, each paired with its sound (phonological form) and meaning (logical form). - a grammar, as a scientific object, is a model of this mental system — specified in formal terms — that captures a speaker’s linguistic competence . - in the principles & parameters and minimalist periods, “grammar” refers to the instantiated version of universal grammar after its parameters have been set by exposure to a particular language. universal grammar note: the idea of universal grammar is essentially this: we observe a phenomenon (observable speech) and ask, “what is happening under the hood? what precedes it?” whatever that underlying mechanism is, we give it a name— universal grammar . this is not so much a formal theory as it is a revolutionary truism, one that points the field toward a particular research direction: becoming more cognitive and biologically oriented. note: chomsky has proposed several models of universal grammar, but universal grammar itself is not a theory. therefore, while individual models can be falsified or revised, universal grammar as a concept remains unaffected. universal grammar → individual grammar (i-language) → observable speech (e-language). grammar = ug (innate principles) + parameter settings (from linguistic experience). universal grammar is the innate, species-specific cognitive system that defines the space of possible human languages, consisting of a set of principles (fixed, universal constraints on grammar) and parameters (limited options that account for cross-linguistic variation). it is part of the human biological endowment, emerges early in development, and enables children to acquire complex grammatical systems rapidly despite limited and imperfect input (the poverty of the stimulus argument). ug serves as the initial state of the language faculty, which interacts with experience to yield a particular language (the steady state ). chomsky like to use the analogy of language growth, not learn because not one is teaching the children. the ug this hypothesis is proposed; because the childrens learn so much; without training, even very complex concepts. research agenda period research program core focus key works central ideas impact / legacy --- --- --- --- --- --- 1950s–1960s generative grammar formal description of syntax as an explicit generative system syntactic structures (1957), aspects of the theory of syntax (1965) language is generated by an internal grammar; competence vs. performance; syntax has deep and surface structures revolutionized linguistics by introducing formal rules and computational modeling of language 1960s–1970s standard theory → extended standard theory refinement of transformations; interface between syntax and semantics aspects (1965), studies on semantics in generative grammar (1972) transformational rules link deep structure (semantic interpretation) and surface structure (phonetic form) integrated syntax with semantics; set the stage for more modular theories 1970s extended standard theory & trace theory greater role for constraints on transformations conditions on transformations (1973) constraints (e.g., island conditions) limit transformations; traces represent moved elements opened path for principles-based grammar rather than rule proliferation 1980–1990s government and binding (gb) theory unified syntactic theory via modules lectures on government and binding (1981) modules: x-bar theory, case theory, binding theory, bounding theory, government, control; principles & parameters framework replaced rule-based grammar with universal principles and language-specific parameters 1990s–present minimalist program reduction of linguistic theory to optimal design the minimalist program (1995) language faculty is an optimal solution given interface constraints; economy principles; derivations driven by feature checking simplified architecture, linking linguistics with cognitive science and biology 1960s–present biolinguistics language as a biological capacity reflections on language (1975), the science of language (2012) language faculty is part of human biology; evolved recently; genetic basis (e.g., foxp2 studies) interdisciplinary field connecting linguistics, biology, psychology, and evolution 1960s–present critique of behaviorism rejection of stimulus-response models of language review of skinner’s verbal behavior (1959) language cannot be explained by conditioning; requires internal mental representations helped spark the cognitive revolution in psychology 1960s–present philosophy of mind & cognitive laws) promoted biologically grounded linguistics and computational minimalism 2005 three factors in language design biolinguistics / minimalism proposed three-factor model: genetic minimalism formalization of phase theory and labeling technical elaboration of minimalist operations like merge can chomsky be categorized as someone from the symbolic view of cognitive science? - chomsky does not commit to the idea that mental computation must be physically symbolic (as in gofai ai); he sees the symbolic model as a theoretical abstraction . - in the minimalist program , he sometimes frames the language faculty in terms of optimal design and interface conditions, which can be interpreted in a more abstract, less mechanistic way. - he has been critical of connectionism and subsymbolic models when they lack explanatory depth or fail to capture the discrete, combinatorial nature of language. references - noam chomsky (1928 – ) [great review of chomsky academic work] - notes.title: Paul Romer
notes.text: paul romer paul romer is known for his significant contributions to economic growth theory and innovation. some of his primary papers include: 1. "endogenous technological change" (1990) : in this seminal paper published in the journal of political economy, romer introduced the concept of endogenous growth theory. he argued that technological progress is not exogenous but rather determined by economic factors such as investment in research and development, human capital accumulation, and knowledge spillovers. this paper laid the foundation for understanding how policies and institutions influence long-term economic growth. 2. "increasing returns and long-run growth" (1986) : this paper, also published in the journal of political economy, explores the role of increasing returns to scale in driving sustained economic growth. romer demonstrates how positive feedback loops can lead to autonomous growth dynamics, challenging the traditional assumption of diminishing returns in economic models. 3. "growth based on increasing returns due to specialization" (1987) : in this paper, romer further develops the concept of increasing returns to scale by focusing on the role of specialization and knowledge accumulation. he highlights how economies can benefit from specialization and trade, leading to higher productivity and growth. 4. "the origins of endogenous growth" (1994) : this paper, co-authored with diego puga, provides an overview of endogenous growth theory's historical and theoretical foundations. romer and puga discuss key contributions to the field and highlight the implications of endogenous growth for understanding the dynamics of technological change and economic development. 5. "economic growth" (2007) : romer's work on economic growth is also encapsulated in his textbook "economic growth," which provides a comprehensive overview of theories, empirical evidence, and policy implications related to economic growth. the book synthesizes romer's research and other economists' contributions, making it a valuable resource for students and researchers in the field. these papers and contributions have profoundly impacted the study of economic growth and development, influencing academic research and policy debates. romer's insights have helped shape our understanding of the drivers of long-term prosperity and the role of innovation in fostering economic progress.

notes.title: Philip Kotler
notes.text: philip kotler philip kotler, often referred to as the "father of modern marketing," is an influential figure in the field of marketing, having authored numerous seminal books and articles throughout his career. some of his main works include: 1. "marketing management" : considered his magnum opus, this book is one of the world's most widely used graduate-level textbooks in marketing. it covers a wide range of marketing principles, theories, and practices. 2. "principles of marketing" : co-authored with gary armstrong, this book is another widely used text that lays out fundamental marketing concepts and strategies for undergraduate students. 3. "kotler on marketing" : this book summarizes kotler's insights on approaching marketing as an integrated set of tools and processes. it offers a concise overview of his marketing philosophy. 4. "marketing 4.0: moving from traditional to digital" : co-authored with hermawan kartajaya and iwan setiawan, this work explores the shift from traditional to digital marketing, emphasizing the importance of technology and online platforms in modern marketing strategies. 5. "marketing insights from a to z: 80 concepts every manager needs to know" : this book provides a comprehensive overview of essential marketing concepts in a concise and accessible format, making it useful for managers and professionals. 6. "marketing 3.0: from products to customers to the human spirit" : also co-authored with hermawan kartajaya and iwan setiawan, this book discusses how marketing has evolved to focus on values and social responsibility, going beyond traditional product-centric approaches. 7. "strategic marketing for nonprofit organizations" : this work applies marketing concepts and strategies to nonprofit organizations, addressing their unique challenges and opportunities. 8. "social marketing: improving the quality of life" : co-authored with ned roberto and nancy lee, this book explores how marketing principles can promote social change and improve public health, safety, and the environment. 9. "the marketing of nations: a strategic approach to building national wealth" : in this book, kotler applies marketing principles to countries and analyzes how nations can improve their competitiveness in the global market. 10. "chaotics: the business of managing and marketing in the age of turbulence" : co-authored with john a. caslione, this book addresses strategies for businesses to navigate and thrive in turbulent economic times. philip kotler's works have profoundly impacted the marketing field, offering foundational theories, practical strategies, and forward-thinking insights into the evolving landscape of marketing and business strategy. references - philip kotler

notes.title: Pieter de la Court
notes.text: pieter de la court pieter de la court was a dutch economist and political theorist in the 17th century. he was known for his contributions to early economic thought and his advocacy for free trade and republican government. here is a table summarizing some of his main ideas: idea description --- --- free trade de la court was a strong proponent of free trade, arguing that allowing the free flow of goods and services leads to greater prosperity and economic growth. against monopolies he criticized monopolies and mercantilist policies, believing they stifled competition and innovation and were detrimental to economic progress. economic liberty de la court emphasized the importance of economic liberty, advocating for minimal government intervention in economic affairs to allow individuals to pursue their interests and maximize wealth. republicanism he advocated for republican forms of government, arguing that they were more conducive to freedom and economic prosperity than monarchies. separation of powers de la court believed in the separation of powers within government to prevent any branch from becoming too powerful and protect individual liberties. meritocracy he supported the idea of meritocracy, where individuals should rise to positions of power and influence based on their abilities and achievements rather than birthright or social status. population and prosperity de la court argued that a large, dynamic population was crucial for a country's prosperity, and he promoted policies that would encourage population growth and economic activity. role of cities he viewed cities as vital centers of trade, industry, and innovation, essential for a nation's economic development and cultural life. education and knowledge de la court believed in the importance of education and the dissemination of knowledge as foundations for economic and social progress. peace and stability he argued that peace and political stability were necessary conditions for economic growth, as they created an environment where trade and industry could flourish. critique of nobility de la court was critical of the nobility and aristocratic privileges, viewing them as impediments to economic and social progress. these ideas reflect pieter de la court's forward-thinking approach to economics and governance, emphasizing free markets, individual liberty, and republican principles as pathways to prosperity and stability. references - pieter de la court

notes.title: Richard Cantillon
notes.text: richard cantillon richard cantillon, an influential 18th-century economist, is known for his seminal work, "essai sur la nature du commerce en général" (essay on the nature of commerce in general). land is the source or matter from which all wealth is drawn; man's labor provides the form for its production, and wealth in itself is nothing but the food, conveniences, and pleasures of life. (cantillon 1755, p. 21. emphasis added) his contributions laid foundational concepts in economics. here is a table summarizing the main ideas from his work: main idea description --- --- entrepreneurial role cantillon emphasized the role of entrepreneurs as risk-bearers who organize production and drive economic activity. cantillon effect he introduced the concept that changes in the money supply affect different groups differently, impacting prices and income distribution. market clearing he discussed the idea of market equilibrium, where prices adjust to balance supply and demand. land rent theory cantillon theorized that land rent is a residual income after deducting production costs, influencing land use and distribution. circulation of money he explored how money circulates through the economy, affecting prices and economic activity. value and price formation cantillon analyzed how the value of goods and services is determined by market forces and how prices adjust accordingly. role of population he noted that population growth impacts economic development, influencing demand, labor supply, and land use. distribution of wealth cantillon examined how wealth is distributed among different social classes and its impact on economic stability. economic uncertainty he highlighted the importance of uncertainty and its influence on economic decisions and entrepreneurship. government and market while not extensively, he touched upon the role of government intervention and its effects on market efficiency. these ideas form the core of cantillon's contributions to economic theory and have influenced subsequent economic thought. references - richard cantillon

headings.text: **Integration with Law, Politics, and the Economy**

notes.text: roberto mangabeira unger roberto mangabeira unger is a brazilian philosopher, legal theorist, and politician whose social theory is one of the most ambitious and original in contemporary thought. his work spans law, politics, economics, and philosophy, and it resists conventional ideological categorization. unger’s core contribution is the idea that social reality is plastic, mutable, and subject to radical innovation —a view he calls "formative context" theory and "radical institutionalism." ideas main idea/concept description --- --- empowered democracy advocates for deepening democracy by increasing citizen participation and decentralizing power. plasticity of social institutions emphasizes that social structures and institutions are malleable and can be reshaped by human action. radical reformism proposes comprehensive and transformative reforms to address systemic social and economic issues. imagination and innovation stresses the importance of creativity and innovation in driving social and economic progress. critique of neoliberalism criticizes neoliberal policies for exacerbating inequalities and limiting democratic control. alternative globalization advocates for a form of globalization that prioritizes social justice, environmental sustainability, and equitable development. human empowerment focuses on empowering individuals through education, technology, and economic opportunities. social solidarity emphasizes the need for social cohesion and collective action to address common challenges. social theory formative contexts unger argues that every society is shaped by formative contexts —deeply embedded institutional and imaginative frameworks that define the limits of social, economic, and political life. unlike structuralist or marxist thinkers, unger believes these contexts are not fixed but radically revisable . human societies are not constrained by immutable laws but are open to deep innovation . these include: - legal and institutional structures (e.g., property, contract, government) - social hierarchies and norms - prevailing ideologies and narratives plasticity of the social “there is no natural or necessary form of social life.” this means that human institutions and practices are inherently malleable , and we can rebuild society in alternative ways through imaginative thought and political action. false necessity and institutional alternatives in his seminal book false necessity: anti-necessitarian social theory in the service of radical democracy (1987), unger argues that: - many social structures are presented as necessary or inevitable (e.g., capitalism, nation-states, legal frameworks) - these necessities are "false" , sustained by ideology and inertia rather than logic or nature - we must explore alternative institutional forms —especially those that deepen democratic participation , flatten hierarchies , and promote self-realization empowered democracy unger calls for an "empowered democracy," which: - goes beyond liberal democracy - involves radical experimentation with new forms of political, economic, and social organization - requires institutional innovations like: - rotating leadership - decentralized decision-making - flexible property regimes - educational systems fostering creative and critical capabilities non-ideal theory with a utopian aim unlike most analytic political philosophers who work within "ideal theory" (e.g., rawls), unger: - works in a "non-ideal" but aspirational mode - tries to imagine and design real alternatives , not just describe justice in theory - believes political imagination is a central intellectual tool —we must design new futures, not just critique the present integration with law, politics, and the economy unger was a key figure in the critical legal studies movement , and much of his early work challenges the neutrality and objectivity of legal reasoning. he integrates his social theory with: - law : law is both a tool of reproduction and a site of creative disruption. - politics : calls for "high-energy politics" —where citizens are engaged in continuous institutional redesign. - economy : advocates for democratizing the market by introducing cooperative, decentralized, and innovative economic models . notable works in social theory - knowledge and politics (1975) - law in modern society (1976) - false necessity (1987) – vol. 1 of politics: a work in constructive social theory - plasticity into power (1987) - democracy realized (1998) phrases - defiance is not always rewarded, but obedience is invariably punished . - human nature & the plasticity of the self - "we are not stuck being the way we are. the human self is not a thing; it is a project." - "human nature is not fixed but formed in history and capable of being reformed by it." - "to be human is to live incompletely—to exist as a being who must make itself." - "each of us is more than the roles society assigns us." - "no social order has the right to claim the entirety of the human personality." - structure, agency, and social transformation - "structures enable and constrain, but they can also be remade." - "the true radicalism is institutional: to reorganize the arrangements of social life to widen the range of human possibility." - "the point is not to destroy structures, but to loosen their grip and multiply their alternatives." - "we must make institutions that give form to our power to reshape them." - democracy, freedom, and empowerment - "democracy should not just redistribute power; it should revolutionize how power is organized." - "to be free is to be capable of reshaping the world, not merely choosing among pre-made options." - "democracy is not only about voting—it is about structure-changing freedom in everyday life." - "we are not truly free if we are locked into inherited roles and routines." - alternative modernity / revolutionary reform - "there is more than one way to be modern." - "we must imagine modernity as the field of possible futures, not the end of history." - "radical change is not necessarily revolutionary upheaval; it can be cumulative, piecemeal, and experimental." - "the task is not to destroy modern institutions but to deepen and democratize them." - "a high-energy democracy requires institutional innovation, not just moral will." - legal theory and institutional imagination - "the law should be a liberating instrument, not a mirror of existing power." - "legal analysis is sterile unless joined to the imagination of alternative institutional forms." - "we should treat law not as a reflection of society but as a tool for its transformation." - education and the formation of the self - notes.title: San Isidoro de Sevilla
notes.text: san isidoro de sevilla san isidoro de sevilla was a distinguished scholar, bishop, and doctor of the church, renowned for his pivotal role in compiling and preserving vast arrays of knowledge during the early middle ages, culminating in his masterwork, the "etymologiae.” isidore of seville, a scholar and theologian of the early middle ages, is best known for his extensive encyclopedic work, "etymologiae" (or "origines"). this work is considered one of the earliest encyclopedias in western civilization and was a crucial reference for medieval scholars. principal works by isidore of seville include: 1. etymologiae (the etymologies) : isidore's most famous and influential work, the "etymologiae" is an encyclopedia that aimed to compile all available knowledge at the time. it covers many subjects, including theology, grammar, geography, medicine, etc. the work is structured around the etymology of words, through which isidore sought to understand and explain the world. 2. de natura rerum (on the nature of things) : before the "etymologiae," isidore wrote "de natura rerum," a book on astronomy and natural history. it was one of the early christian treatments of science and sought to reconcile classical knowledge with christian doctrine. 3. historia de regibus gothorum, vandalorum et suevorum (history of the kings of the goths, vandals, and suevi) : this history of the gothic, vandal, and suevian kings is a valuable resource for understanding the early history of these peoples in iberia. 4. chronica maiora (the great chronicle) : this work is a universal history that begins with creation and runs to isidore's present day. it incorporates much of the content from his "history of the kings of the goths, vandals, and suevi." 5. differentiarum libri (books of differences) : this includes two works, "differentiae verborum," which distinguishes between synonyms, and "differentiae spirituales," which deals with ethical and spiritual concepts. 6. sententiae (sentences) : this theological treatise is divided into three books and deals with the doctrines of the trinity, ecclesiology, and christian ethics. isidore's works were highly influential throughout the middle ages, serving as a cornerstone for medieval scholarship, education, and culture. his efforts to preserve and synthesize knowledge from various sources make him a significant figure in the intellectual history of the west. references - isidoro de sevilla - …

notes.text: sigismund schlomo freud the issue is not freud himself—his work may be an example of bad science—but his followers should know better and treat his views not as a religion, but as an explanatory framework that must be tested. research which were freud main research problems? area research questions --- --- unconscious processes - how much of mental life occurs outside awareness? - what mechanisms govern unconscious thought? - how do unconscious processes influence conscious behavior and emotions? - how can unconscious content be revealed and studied? instincts and drives - how do sexual (libidinal) and aggressive drives shape mental life? - how are instinctual desires satisfied, repressed, or redirected? - what is the role of drives in motivating behavior and forming personality? mental functioning dynamics - how do the pleasure principle and reality principle regulate thought and action? - how does the mind manage tension between instinctual desires and external constraints? - what mechanisms underlie repression, resistance, and defense? personality development - how do early childhood experiences shape adult personality? - what is the impact of psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital) on behavior? - how do family dynamics and parental relationships influence mental and emotional development? psychopathology - what psychic conflicts produce anxiety, hysteria, or neuroses? - how does repression generate psychological symptoms? - what are the roles of defense mechanisms in protecting the ego? - how do early traumas or unresolved conflicts affect later mental health? dreams and symbolism - how do dreams reveal unconscious desires? - what processes (condensation, displacement, symbolization) transform latent thoughts into manifest content? - can dreams provide insight into unresolved conflicts or repressed material? psychoanalytic methods - how can free association uncover unconscious material? - what is the significance of slips of the tongue, jokes, and parapraxes? - how can clinical observation be systematized into a general theory of the mind? - how can psychoanalytic techniques be validated scientifically? mental energy and motivation - how is psychic energy (libido) distributed and transformed? - what is the relationship between energy, tension, and behavior? - how do mental processes conserve or expend energy in different contexts? interpersonal and social influences - how do social interactions and relationships shape personality? - what is the role of cultural norms in regulating instinctual drives? - how do authority, attachment, and family structure influence mental development? model which models does freud used in his works? target system model description --- notes.title: Sir Robert Gordon Menzies
notes.text: sir robert gordon menzies sir robert menzies, as prime minister of australia for a significant period from 1939 to 1966, had a notable impact on australia's industrial policy during his tenure. here are some key aspects of his industrial policy : 1. protectionism : menzies' government generally favored protectionist policies to nurture domestic industries and shield them from international competition. this approach was in line with the prevailing economic philosophy of the time, which prioritized domestic manufacturing and industrial self-sufficiency. 2. tariffs and trade : menzies implemented policies that increased tariffs on imported goods, aiming to protect australian industries from foreign competition. this protectionist stance was particularly evident in sectors such as manufacturing, agriculture, and textiles. 3. support for key industries : menzies' government provided various forms of support to key industries deemed vital for the country's economic development. this support included subsidies, grants, and other forms of financial assistance to stimulate growth and innovation in strategic sectors. 4. labor relations : menzies' government maintained a stance that generally favored employers in industrial relations matters. it sought to maintain stability in the labor market and minimize disruptions through policies that often favored the interests of businesses over those of organized labor. 5. infrastructure development : menzies' government invested in infrastructure projects to support industrial development, including transportation networks, energy infrastructure, and telecommunications. these investments aimed to facilitate the efficient movement of goods and services, as well as to provide essential utilities for industrial activities. 6. encouragement of foreign investment : while advocating for protectionist measures, menzies also recognized the importance of foreign investment in stimulating economic growth. his government encouraged foreign companies to invest in australia, particularly in sectors where domestic capital was insufficient to fund large-scale projects. 7. focus on economic growth : overall, menzies' industrial policy was guided by a broader focus on promoting economic growth and development. his government sought to create an environment conducive to business investment, innovation, and job creation, with the goal of enhancing australia's overall prosperity. while menzies' industrial policies reflected the economic priorities and challenges of his time, they have been subject to scrutiny and debate in subsequent years, particularly regarding their long-term impact on australia's industrial landscape and economic competitiveness. references - sir robert gordon notes.text: thomas sowell work year work type description --- --- --- --- 1970 say’s law: an historical analysis book economic theory; refutation and analysis of say’s law. 1972 economic theory: an introduction book introductory economics; formal presentation of micro and macroeconomic principles. 1974 knowledge and decisions book economics of information, decision-making in society; knowledge distribution. 1975 race and economics book examines economic disparities among races; historical and policy analysis. 1981 markets and minorities book market functioning and minority groups; economic opportunities and discrimination. 1983 the economics and politics of race book extended treatment of racial economic issues and policy implications. 1987 a conflict of visions: ideological origins of political struggles book political philosophy; contrasting visions shaping social policy debates. 1988 civil rights: rhetoric or reality? book critical analysis of the civil rights movement’s economic and social outcomes. 1990 knowledge and decisions (2nd edition) book updated edition with revisions; decision-making and knowledge in complex systems. 1993 race and culture: a world view book cultural factors in economic outcomes; international and historical perspective. 1995 the vision of the anointed: self-congratulation as a basis for social policy book critique of elite policy-making and moralistic governance. 2000 basic economics book comprehensive introduction to economics for general readers; widely used. 2004 applied economics: thinking beyond stage one book real-world applications of economic principles; policy critique. 2007 economic facts and fallacies book addresses common misconceptions in economics; data-driven analysis. 2010 dismantling america: and other controversial essays book collection of essays on social, economic, and political issues. 2015 wealth, poverty and politics: an international perspective book explores factors behind global wealth disparities; geography, culture, politics. 2018 charter schools and their enemies book analysis of education policy; evaluation of charter school effectiveness. knowledge and decisions sowell’s knowledge and decisions powerfully illustrates how dispersed knowledge shapes economic and political outcomes, but his framework has limits. by privileging local problem-solving, he under-theorizes the hierarchical and systemic nature of many real-world challenges. problems differ not only by scale but by interdependence—ranging from personal choices to infrastructural or societal systems. this localist bias leaves his framework less capable of addressing questions of institutional design, such as subsidies for emerging industries, where structured, rule-based coordination is necessary. in short, sowell explains why central planning fails, but provides little guidance for how societies should design intermediate institutions to handle complex, large-scale problems. pre - analysis knowledge is a structured representation of reality that allows an agent—human, artificial, or otherwise—to make reliable inferences, predictions, or decisions. it encompasses information that has been validated, justified, or otherwise confirmed as dependable within a given context. knowledge is fundamentally about how an observer is able to describe or act in the world. problems and decisions can be categorized by their complexity and by the number of actors involved in working toward their solution. book the book is an extension of hayek’s work “on the use of knowledge in society”. it primarily discusses descriptive knowledge, which enables informed decision-making. knowledge and decisions is a rigorous exploration of how knowledge is dispersed in society and how this affects economic, political, and social decision-making. sowell argues that no single individual or centralized authority can possess all the knowledge needed to make optimal decisions; instead, knowledge is often decentralized, context-specific, and tacit. he examines the mechanisms—markets, organizations, and political institutions—that enable societies to aggregate dispersed knowledge and make effective decisions despite inherent limitations. key themes: 1. dispersed knowledge: knowledge exists in fragments across individuals and cannot be fully centralized. 2. decision-making constraints: institutions and social systems must cope with limited knowledge and imperfect information. 3. trade-offs in coordination: centralized vs. decentralized decision-making, efficiency vs. control. 4. role of incentives: proper incentives and feedback mechanisms are crucial to harness dispersed knowledge. 5. limits of expertise: expertise cannot replace the collective information embedded in society. analysis the framing of knowledge in this book is problematic. knowledge enables us to make decisions and solve problems, but sowell treats decisions or problems almost always from a local perspective - or approximately hierarchical equal. in reality, problems exist on a spectrum—ranging from highly local issues (e.g., what type of coffee to buy) to less local or large-scale challenges (e.g., how to repair a city’s sewage system ). in other words, decisions and problems exist within a hierarchy in terms of the systems - and ecosystems that compose organize living; or by the amount of people that are interested - affected by them. let’s consider how, within the framework proposed by this book, subsidies are treated. for instance, when examining subsidies granted to an emerging industry under a defined set of rules—essentially a management framework—it appears that the book does not provide a clear or specific answer to this type of question or problem. this limitation in sowell’s framework can be further developed under the theme of the limits of self-organization . references - https://www.amazon.com/-/es/thomas-sowell/dp/b017v8g6xs - https://archive.org/details/knowledgedecisio00sowe 0 - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/thomas sowellecibi

notes.title: Vannevar Bush
notes.text: vannevar bush vannevar bush was a seminal american engineer, inventor, and science administrator, known for his profound influence on the direction of scientific research in the united states during and after world war ii. here are some of his main works and contributions: 1. "as we may think" : this seminal essay, published in "the atlantic monthly" in 1945, speculated on the future of information storage and retrieval, proposing a machine called the "memex." the memex was envisioned as a mechanical desk that could store books, records, and communications, and it's notably prescient of modern-day personal computers and the internet. 2. the manhattan project : although not a direct creator, bush was instrumental in the administration and funding of the manhattan project through his role as the head of the office of scientific research and development (osrd). he coordinated the efforts of military, industrial, and scientific communities during wwii. 3. osrd (office of scientific research and development) : bush directed this office, which was responsible for the majority of wartime scientific research efforts, including the development of radar and other critical military technologies. the osrd effectively connected the scientific community with the military needs of the u.s. during the war. 4. the national science foundation (nsf) : following wwii, bush authored a report titled "science, the endless frontier," which led to the creation of the national science foundation. this report laid the groundwork for post-war science policies and emphasized the importance of federal funding for scientific research, advocating for science as a key to improving public health, national security, and economic prosperity. 5. early computers and digital networking concepts : beyond the memex, bush's vision and technical expertise influenced the development of early computing and digital networking concepts. his ideas foresaw many aspects of information society, including the structure of what would become the internet. vannevar bush's work significantly shaped modern scientific research and development policies, and his vision for technology foresaw the information age decades before it came to fruition. references - vannevar bush

notes.title: William B. Bonvillian
notes.text: william b. bonvillian william b. bonvillian is an influential figure in the fields of science and technology policy, particularly known for his insights on innovation systems and the role of government in fostering technological advancements. here are some of the main ideas and themes found in his work: 1. advanced manufacturing : bonvillian has focused on the importance of advanced manufacturing in the united states, advocating for policies that support the development and adoption of new manufacturing technologies. he argues that revitalizing manufacturing is crucial for economic growth and maintaining competitiveness. 2. innovation system challenges : he examines the challenges within the u.s. innovation system, particularly the gaps between research breakthroughs and their commercialization. bonvillian stresses the need for improved mechanisms to bridge this 'valley of death', ensuring that innovations can move from the lab to the marketplace effectively. 3. role of federal r&d : bonvillian has explored the role of federal research and development (r&d) programs in driving technological innovation. he argues for strategic adjustments in federal r&d to better support areas critical to national interests and economic leadership, such as energy and biotechnology. 4. educational reforms for innovation : he advocates for educational reforms that better align with the needs of an innovation-based economy. this includes enhancing stem (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) education and integrating skills that promote creativity and innovation in problem-solving. 5. policy for science and technology : bonvillian’s work also delves into specific policy recommendations for supporting science and technology development. he has contributed to discussions on how policies can be structured to support emerging technologies, how to structure government-industry partnerships, and the importance of innovation in addressing societal challenges like healthcare and climate change. william b. bonvillian's contributions are particularly valued for their practical implications, offering guidance on how policies can be crafted and implemented to better support technological innovation and economic growth. references - william b. bonvillian

notes.title: William Petty
notes.text: william petty sure, here’s a table summarizing the main theories of william petty, a notable economist and statistician from the 17th century: theory description --- --- political arithmetic petty's approach to economic and social analysis using quantitative data to inform policy decisions. he emphasized the importance of empirical data collection and statistical analysis. labour theory of value the idea that the value of goods is derived from the amount of labor required to produce them. petty believed that labor was the fundamental source of value. full employment petty argued for policies to achieve full employment, believing it was essential for economic stability and growth. he advocated for public works and other measures to ensure that everyone who wanted to work could find a job. land and rent theory petty theorized that the value of land and its rent was based on its productivity and location. he introduced the concept of "economic rent," which is the income derived from the ownership of land and other natural resources. quantity theory of money he suggested that the amount of money in circulation in an economy is directly proportional to the level of prices, which is an early formulation of the quantity theory of money. national income accounting petty was one of the pioneers in estimating national income and wealth, laying the groundwork for modern national income accounting and gdp calculations. population and economic growth he believed that population growth was a crucial factor for economic prosperity and that a larger population could contribute to greater economic output and development. these theories collectively contributed to the development of classical economics and the field of political economy. references - buck, peter. notes.title: Zhuge Liang
notes.text: zhuge liang zhuge liang (181–234 ce), also known as kongming (孔明), was a renowned chinese statesman, military strategist, engineer, and scholar during the three kingdoms period. his ideas span military tactics, governance, ethics, and philosophy. 🧠 zhuge liang's core ideas 1. strategic wisdom (兵法 bīngfǎ) - caution over aggression : zhuge advocated strategic patience , using diplomacy, alliances, and deception over brute force. - "empty fort strategy" : a psychological tactic where weakness is masked as strength to deter enemies—illustrating his belief in using intelligence over force. - flexibility : emphasized adapting plans to changing conditions—a principle resembling sun tzu’s teachings. 2. meritocratic governance - promoted officials based on talent and virtue , not lineage or loyalty. - wrote the "chu shi biao" (出师表) —a memorial to emperor liu shan advising good governance, loyalty to the people, and restraint in the use of power. 3. moral leadership (仁政 rénzhèng) - argued that legitimacy comes from benevolence, ethical rule, and the people’s welfare . - saw the ruler’s job as a moral guide, not just a sovereign. - believed in internal discipline and moral self-cultivation for administrators. 4. administrative efficiency - reformed shu han’s bureaucracy with focus on: - clear legal codes. - fair tax systems. - anti-corruption measures. - emphasized responsibility and accountability , believing in detailed record-keeping and supervision. 5. technological and logistical ingenuity - credited with inventions like the "wooden ox" (木牛流马) —a kind of wheelbarrow for food transport. - master of logistics: ensured sustained supply lines during long campaigns. 6. long-term vision - advocated a gradualist approach to reunifying china, seeing sustainability more important than short-term victories. - repeatedly warned against rash military action without thorough planning. 📜 famous quotes (translated): - “opportunities multiply as they are seized.” - “those who are benevolent are invincible.” - “do not be ashamed of mistakes and thus make them crimes.” 📚 influence zhuge liang is often cited alongside confucius for his moral teachings and alongside sun tzu for his military acumen. his ideas remain relevant in: - leadership and organizational ethics. - military academies (strategy and logistics). - chinese political thought and folklore.

notes.title: Notes corpus
notes.text: notes corpus long-form notes for the naturgnosis note module ( /note/ ): catalog at /note/ , single-note viewer at /note/note.html?n=<path . this directory is the source of truth — hand-edited markdown, never machine-edited. after any change, rebuild the search index and commit it: python bin/build note index.py format - a note is a markdown file ( .md ), rendered on the fly by the viewer. no metadata required: the title comes from the first # heading (else the filename); the top-level directory is the section. optional tags go in --- front matter (same style as epistecnica; only tags: [...] is read, everything else ignored): --- tags: [social-space, method] --- - a live note is a self-contained, hand-authored html page ( .html ) with bespoke interactivity and its own scripts. served as-is, never rendered through the viewer; the catalog still indexes it (title, headings, text) and links straight to the page with a live chip. no cdn libraries allowed in live notes. naming convention note paths (directories and .md / .html filenames) must be: - ascii only — a-z , 0-9 , - (no accents, spaces, underscores, dots beyond the .md / .html extension) - lowercase — never capitals - kebab-case — words separated by - examples: social-space-overview.md , technique-glossary.md . non-markdown assets (images, code samples) may live beside notes and are exempt from the filename rule, but directories always follow it. canonical slug (epistecnica parity): nfkd-normalize to ascii, lowercase, every run of non-alphanumeric characters becomes a single - , trim leading/trailing - ; collisions get a -2 , -3 , … suffix. never run bin/slugify files.py (underscore rule) on this directory. bin/build note index.py validates every note path and tag, prints warnings with the suggested normalized form for violations, and never fails the build. keep the output warning-free. pins catalog pins (starred notes) are server-side, stored as a single pins document in the naturgnosis couchdb database via get/post /note/api/pins (see bin/sync.py ). the catalog hides pin ui when the api is unreachable (e.g. sync.py --no-couch ).

notes.title: Research Group
notes.text: research group "research groups" as quasi-firms refer to the concept where research groups within academic institutions or other organizations operate similarly to firms. they exhibit characteristics such as: 1. autonomy : research groups often have a degree of operational independence, making decisions on research directions, project management, and resource allocation. 2. funding and resources : like firms, they compete for funding from various sources, manage budgets, and allocate resources to different projects. 3. leadership and hierarchy : they typically have a leadership structure with a principal investigator (pi) or group leader who acts similarly to a firm's ceo, making strategic decisions and guiding the group's research agenda. 4. outputs and outcomes : their performance is often measured by outputs such as publications, patents, and other research contributions analogous to a firm's products and services. 5. collaboration and competition : research groups collaborate with other groups and institutions, but they also compete for funding, talent, and recognition in their field, similar to firms in a market. 6. incentives and rewards : members of research groups may be motivated by incentives such as career advancement, recognition, and financial rewards, paralleling the incentive structures in firms. references - etzkowitz, h. (2003). research groups as ‘quasi-firms’: the invention of the entrepreneurial university. 32(1), 109–121.
